entry.title: Stay on the Manifold: Hierarchical Bayesian Trajectory-Family Transfer for Sparse-Target Reconstruction and Sampling

link.title: Stay on the Manifold: Hierarchical Bayesian Trajectory-Family Transfer for Sparse-Target Reconstruction and Sampling

entry.content: Where should reconstructions and new samples lie when a few observations reveal only fragments of a trajectory? We propose hierarchical Bayesian trajectory principal-manifold sampling (HB-TPM), which learns a family of smooth curves from ordered source tasks and adapts it to sparse targets. For unordered vectors, alternating progression assignments and coefficient updates estimate trajectory structure between and beyond the observed shots under the learned source family. Observation-aware extensions connect the trajectory prior to photon arrivals and image-encoded cardiac cycles. Our analysis characterizes the coefficient directions supplied by the prior and bounds sampling error conditional on curve recovery. Across 30 held-out vector tasks, HB-TPM reduces mean sliced-Wasserstein distance by 21.0-41.8% relative to a source-adapted VAE. Prior-strength and sampling ablations identify coefficient shrinkage as the main supported mechanism. On 100 simulated photon records, adaptation lowers mean relative trajectory RMSE by 50.2% versus target-only fitting and 23.6% versus source-mean prediction. Across three training seeds and five folds on 98 cardiac sequences, HB-TPM with latent-MSE training achieves the best mean reconstruction among the tested configurations. Together, the results demonstrate trajectory-family transfer for sparse-target reconstruction and trajectory-centered sampling when source and target tasks share comparable progression structure.

entry.title: Optimal Forecast Reconciliation with Uncertainty Quantification

link.title: Optimal Forecast Reconciliation with Uncertainty Quantification

entry.content: We propose to estimate the weight matrix used for forecast reconciliation as parameters in a general linear model in order to quantify its uncertainty. This implies that forecast reconciliation can be formulated as an orthogonal projection from the space of base-forecast errors into a coherent linear subspace. We use variance decomposition together with the Wishart distribution to derive the central estimator for the forecast-error covariance matrix. In addition, we prove that distance-reducing properties apply to the reconciled forecasts at all levels of the hierarchy as well as to the forecast-error covariance. A covariance matrix for the reconciliation weight matrix is derived, which leads to improved estimates of the forecast-error covariance matrix. We show how shrinkage can be introduced in the formulated model by imposing specific priors on the weight matrix and the forecast-error covariance matrix. The method is illustrated in a simulation study that shows consistent improvements in the log-score. Finally, standard errors for the weight matrix and the variance-separation formula are illustrated using a case study of forecasting electricity load in Sweden.

entry.title: Coherent forecast combination for linearly constrained multiple time series

link.title: Coherent forecast combination for linearly constrained multiple time series

entry.content: Forecasting linearly constrained multiple time series, as those arising in National Accounts, energy systems and supply chain planning, requires that the forecasts of all variables jointly satisfy the underlying accounting or resource-balance identities. When several experts provide forecasts for some or all of the variables, classical forecast combination operates on each variable and ignores the linear constraints, while forecast reconciliation enforces such constraints by using a single forecast per variable. To bridge this gap, we develop an original coherent forecast combination framework, in which the joint problem of combination across experts and coherence across variables is formulated as a linearly constrained optimization problem. Closed-form expressions are derived for the coherent combined forecast and its error covariance matrix, and the statistical properties of the resulting estimators are discussed. A Monte Carlo experiment and a forecasting application to an Australian daily electricity generation dataset confirm that the proposed approach significantly improves forecast accuracy with respect to standard forecast combination and reconciliation alternatives.

entry.title: Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging for uncertainty quantification of electricity price forecasts

link.title: Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging for uncertainty quantification of electricity price forecasts

entry.content: Quantifying the uncertainty of forecasting models is essential to assess and mitigate the risks associated with data-driven decisions, especially in volatile domains such as electricity markets. In this paper, we propose a computationally efficient isotonic variant of Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA), called Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging (iQRA), for generating probabilistic forecasts from ensembles of point forecasts. Building on QRA, we introduce stochastic order constraints as a hyperparameter-free regularization mechanism that reduces computational complexity while maintaining competitive forecast accuracy. We further demonstrate that the same isotonic regularization principle can be applied to the smoothed estimator of QRA. In an extensive forecasting study of two European day-ahead electricity markets, we show that iQRA and its smoothed variant consistently rank among the top state-of-the-art postprocessing methods in terms of reliability and sharpness. It produces well-calibrated prediction intervals, with smoothed iQRA providing superior reliability even when compared against coverage-oriented conformal prediction. We further introduce a battery arbitrage evaluation, showing that the leading probabilistic methods achieve the highest profit per trade and that probabilistic risk control improves the economic value of trading decisions. Isotonic regularization offers a scalable hyperparameter-free variable selection for linear quantile regression, making iQRA attractive for practical decision-support systems in energy markets.

entry.title: Causal Representation Learning from Multimodal Clinical Records under Non-Random Modality Missingness

link.title: Causal Representation Learning from Multimodal Clinical Records under Non-Random Modality Missingness

entry.content: Clinical notes contain rich patient information, such as diagnoses or medications, making them valuable for patient representation learning. Recent advances in large language models have further improved the ability to extract meaningful representations from clinical texts. However, clinical notes are often missing. For example, in our MIMIC-IV cohort, 35.15% of patients have no eligible discharge summaries. In such cases, representations can be learned from other modalities such as structured data, chest X-rays, or radiology reports. Yet the availability of these modalities is influenced by clinical decision-making and varies across patients, potentially producing modality missing-not-at-random (MMNAR) patterns. We propose a causal representation learning framework that leverages observed data and informative missingness in multimodal clinical records. It consists of: (1) an MMNAR-aware modality fusion component that integrates structured data, imaging, and text while conditioning on missingness patterns to capture patient health and clinician-driven assignment; (2) a modality reconstruction component with latent alignment to preserve modality information in the learned representation; and (3) a multitask outcome prediction model with a rectifier that corrects for residual bias from specific modality observation patterns. Comprehensive evaluations across MIMIC-IV and eICU show consistent gains over the strongest baselines, achieving relative AUC improvements of up to 4.3% for hospital readmission and 2.7% for ICU admission.

entry.title: postcard: An R Package for Marginal Effect Estimation with or without Prognostic Score Adjustment

link.title: postcard: An R Package for Marginal Effect Estimation with or without Prognostic Score Adjustment

entry.content: Covariate adjustment is a widely used technique in randomized clinical trials (RCTs) for improving the efficiency of treatment effect estimators. By adjusting for predictive baseline covariates, variance can be reduced, enhancing statistical precision and study power. Rosenblum and van der Laan [2010] use the framework of generalized linear models (GLMs) in a plug-in analysis to show efficiency gains using covariate adjustment for marginal effect estimation. Recently the use of prognostic scores as adjustment covariates has gained popularity. Schuler et al. [2022] introduce and validate the method for continuous endpoints using linear models. Building on this work H{\o}jbjerre-Frandsen et al. [2025] extends the method proposed by Schuler et al. [2022] to be used in combination with the GLM plug-in procedure [Rosenblum and van der Laan, 2010]. This method achieves semi-parametric efficiency under assumptions of additive treatment effects on the link scale. Additionally, H{\o}jbjerre-Frandsen et al. [2025] provide a formula for power approximation which is valid even under model misspecification, enabling realistic sample size estimation. This article introduces an R package, which implements the GLM plug-in method with or without PrOgnoSTic CovARiate aDjustment, postcard. The package has two core features: (1) estimating marginal effects and the variance hereof (with or without prognostic adjustment) and (2) approximating statistical power. Functionalities also include integration of the Discrete Super Learner for constructing prognostic scores and simulation capabilities for exploring the methods in practice. Through examples and simulations, we demonstrate postcard as a practical toolkit for statisticians.

entry.title: Multi-layer dissolution exponential-family models for weighted signed networks

link.title: Multi-layer dissolution exponential-family models for weighted signed networks

entry.content: Understanding the structure of signed weighted networks is essential for analysing complex systems in which relationships between nodes vary both in sign and strength. Despite significant advances in statistical network analysis, there is still a lack of models that can account for both the sign and the strength of interactions in networks. We introduce a multi-layer dissolution exponential random graph modelling framework that enables systematic assessment of structural balance effects. We adopt a fully-probabilistic hierarchical approach that partially pools information across layers, with parameters estimated via an adaptive approximate exchange algorithm. A simulation study shows that the algorithm recovers the layer-specific parameters with small bias. We demonstrate the flexibility and explanatory power of the proposed methodology through an application to the gene interaction network associated with dilated cardiomyopathy, in which a multi-layer signed structure is constructed by progressively thresholding interaction confidence scores, with edge signs derived from pairwise co-expression. The analysis shows that positive co-expression edges embedded in positive triangles are more likely to persist at higher confidence levels, while negative edges whose endpoints share positive partners, which form unbalanced triangles, are preferentially dissolved as the confidence threshold increases.

entry.title: Conformalized Bayesian Inference, with Applications to Random Partition Models

link.title: Conformalized Bayesian Inference, with Applications to Random Partition Models

entry.content: Bayesian posterior distributions naturally represent parameter uncertainty informed by data. However, when the parameter space is complex, as in many nonparametric settings where it is infinite-dimensional or combinatorially large, standard summaries such as posterior means, credible intervals, or simple notions of multimodality are often unavailable, hindering interpretable posterior uncertainty quantification. We introduce Conformalized Bayesian Inference (CBI), a broadly applicable and computationally efficient framework for posterior inference on nonstandard parameter spaces. CBI yields a point estimate, a credible region with assumption-free posterior coverage guarantees, and a principled analysis of posterior multimodality, requiring only Monte Carlo samples from the posterior and a notion of discrepancy between parameters. The method builds a pseudo-density score for each parameter value, yielding a maximum-a-posteriori-like point estimate and a credible region derived from conformal prediction principles. The key conceptual step underlying this construction is the reinterpretation of posterior inference as prediction on the parameter space, with interesting connections to classical Bayesian point estimation and credible set constructions. A final density-based clustering step identifies representative posterior modes. We investigate a number of theoretical and methodological properties of CBI and demonstrate its practicality, scalability, and versatility in simulated and real data clustering applications with random partition models.

entry.title: Multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression for noisy outputs and non-nested experimental designs: decoupled versus joint likelihood optimization

link.title: Multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression for noisy outputs and non-nested experimental designs: decoupled versus joint likelihood optimization

entry.content: This paper investigates a recursive formulation of auto-regressive multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression in the challenging setting of noisy and non-nested high- and low-fidelity data. We propose a decoupled optimization strategy based on the expectation-maximization algorithm, which exploits the structure of the recursive model. In particular, we derive closed-form update formulas when the scaling factor is modeled as a parametric linear predictor. This approach is compared with the fully coupled likelihood maximization of the classical, non-recursive formulation. A series of benchmark experiments, covering applications of increasing complexity, highlights the performance of both approaches. The results demonstrate that the proposed recursive strategy substantially reduces training time when large low-fidelity datasets are available, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation.

entry.title: Exchangeable Gaussian Processes with application to epidemics

link.title: Exchangeable Gaussian Processes with application to epidemics

entry.content: We develop a Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling collections of related epidemic trajectories using exchangeable Gaussian processes. The proposed formulation induces structured dependence across time-varying transmission processes through shared latent Gaussian process components, leading to interpretable pooling behaviour, variance decompositions and intra-class correlation parameters that quantify information sharing across populations. The framework accommodates both direct and indirect observation regimes, including noisy measurements of effective reproduction numbers, latent transmission models for Chikungunya outbreaks and age-structured epidemic systems driven by partially observed infection dynamics. We discuss connections with broader multi-output Gaussian process formulations, including coregionalisation and latent factor models, while emphasising the interpretation of the proposed approach as a functional random-effects framework for related temporal trajectories. A simulation study investigates the behaviour of the proposed models under varying cross-population dependence structures including dependent, weakly dependent and independent settings. Across several epidemic applications, the proposed models demonstrate strong predictive performance while providing interpretable insights into shared and population-specific transmission dynamics.

entry.title: Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation for a Genuinely Unbalanced Dynamic Network Panel Data Model

link.title: Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation for a Genuinely Unbalanced Dynamic Network Panel Data Model

entry.content: This paper develops quasi-maximum likelihood estimation for genuinely unbalanced dynamic network panel data models. We first study a baseline one-way fixed effect specification and then extend the framework to two-way fixed effects. The model accommodates contemporaneous and lagged network spillovers, temporal dependence, and a listing effect that operates when a unit first appears in the panel. For the baseline specification, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the QMLE, characterize the incidental-parameter bias, and propose a bias-corrected estimator. We further provide a consistent estimator of the asymptotic covariance matrix, to enable feasible inference. Under the two-way fixed effect extension, we derive the corresponding asymptotic distribution, bias correction, and covariance matrix estimator, accounting for the additional bias component induced by the time fixed effects. Monte Carlo simulations examine the finite sample performance of the proposed estimators and inference procedure. An empirical application to Airbnb listings from New Zealand and New York City reveals region-specific patterns in spatial and temporal price transmission, highlighting the importance of modeling genuine unbalancedness in dynamic network settings.

entry.title: Assessment of evidence against homogeneity in exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots

link.title: Assessment of evidence against homogeneity in exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots

entry.content: Exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots are constructed by displaying all subgroup treatment effects of interest against subgroup sample size, providing a useful overview of the observed treatment effect heterogeneity in a clinical trial. As in any exploratory subgroup analysis, however, the observed estimates suffer from small sample sizes and multiplicity issues. To facilitate more interpretable exploratory assessments, this paper introduces a computationally efficient method to generate homogeneity regions within exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots. Using the Doubly Robust (DR) learner, pseudo-outcomes are used to estimate subgroup effects and derive reference distributions, quantifying how surprising observed heterogeneity is under a homogeneous effects model. Explicit formulas are derived for the homogeneity region and different methods for calculation of the critical values are compared. The method is illustrated with a cardiovascular trial and evaluated via simulation, showing well-calibrated inference and improved performance over standard approaches using simple differences of observed group means.

entry.title: CausalCompass: Evaluating the Robustness of Time-Series Causal Discovery in Misspecified Scenarios

link.title: CausalCompass: Evaluating the Robustness of Time-Series Causal Discovery in Misspecified Scenarios

entry.content: Causal discovery from time series is a fundamental task in machine learning. However, its widespread adoption is hindered by a reliance on untestable causal assumptions and by the lack of robustness-oriented evaluation in existing benchmarks. To address these challenges, we propose CausalCompass, a flexible and extensible benchmark framework designed to assess the robustness of time-series causal discovery (TSCD) methods under violations of modeling assumptions. To demonstrate the practical utility of CausalCompass, we conduct extensive benchmarking of representative TSCD algorithms across eight assumption-violation scenarios. Our experimental results indicate that no single method consistently attains optimal performance across all settings. Nevertheless, in most scenarios, the methods exhibiting superior overall performance are deep learning-based approaches. We further provide hyperparameter sensitivity analyses to deepen the understanding of these findings. We additionally conduct ablation experiments to explain the strong performance of deep learning-based methods under assumption violations. We also find that NTS-NOTEARS relies on standardized preprocessing in practice, performing poorly in the vanilla setting but exhibiting strong performance after standardization. Finally, our work aims to provide a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of TSCD methods under assumption violations, thereby facilitating their broader adoption in real-world applications. The user-friendly implementation, documentation and datasets are available at https://github.com/huiyang-yi/CausalCompass.

entry.title: Dynamic Bayesian Predictive Stacking via Markovian Spatiotemporal Propagation

link.title: Dynamic Bayesian Predictive Stacking via Markovian Spatiotemporal Propagation

entry.content: This manuscript develops computationally efficient online learning for multivariate spatiotemporal models. The proposed framework relies on matrix-variate Gaussian distributions, dynamic linear models, and Bayesian predictive stacking to efficiently share information across temporal data shards. The model facilitates effective information propagation over time while seamlessly integrating spatial components within a dynamic framework, building a Markovian dependence structure between datasets at successive time instants. This structure supports flexible, high-dimensional modeling of complex dependence patterns, as commonly found in spatiotemporal phenomena, where computational challenges arise rapidly with increasing dimensions. The proposed approach further manages exact inference through predictive stacking, enhancing robustness and interoperability. Combining sequential and parallel processing of temporal shards, each unit passes assimilated information forward and then back-smooths it to improve posterior estimation, incorporating all available information. This framework advances the scalability and adaptability of spatiotemporal modeling, making it suitable for dynamic, multivariate, and data-rich environments. Simulation experiments and an extracted data analysis from the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (CDSE) help evaluate and illustrate the framework.

entry.title: Competing Risk Analysis in Cardiovascular Outcome Trials: A Simulation Comparison of Cox and Fine-Gray Models

link.title: Competing Risk Analysis in Cardiovascular Outcome Trials: A Simulation Comparison of Cox and Fine-Gray Models

entry.content: Cardiovascular outcome trials commonly face competing risks when non-CV death prevents observation of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). While Cox proportional hazards models treat competing events as independent censoring, Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models explicitly handle competing risks, targeting different estimands. This simulation study using bivariate copula models systematically varies competing event rates (0.5%-5% annually), treatment effects on competing events (50% reduction to 50% increase), and correlation structures to compare these approaches. At competing event rates typical of CV outcome trials (~1% annually), Cox and Fine-Gray produce nearly identical hazard ratio estimates regardless of correlation strength or treatment effect direction. Substantial divergence occurs only with high competing rates and directionally discordant treatment effects, though neither estimator provides unbiased estimates of true marginal hazard ratios under these conditions. In typical CV trial settings with low competing event rates, Cox models remain appropriate for primary analysis due to superior interpretability. Pre-specified Cox models should not be abandoned for competing risk methods. Importantly, Fine-Gray models do not constitute proper sensitivity analyses to Cox models per ICH E9(R1), as they target different estimands rather than testing assumptions. As supplementary analysis, cumulative incidence using Aalen-Johansen estimator can provide transparency about competing risk impact. Under high competing-risk scenarios, alternative approaches such as inverse probability of censoring weighting, multiple imputation, or inclusion of all-cause mortality in primary endpoints warrant consideration.

entry.title: Sparse Probabilistic Richardson Extrapolation

link.title: Sparse Probabilistic Richardson Extrapolation

entry.content: Almost every numerical task can be cast as extrapolation with respect to the fidelity or tolerance parameters of a consistent numerical method. This perspective enables probabilistic uncertainty quantification and optimal experimental design functionality to be deployed, and also unlocks the potential for the convergence of numerical methods to be accelerated. Recent work established Probabilistic Richardson Extrapolation as a proof-of-concept, demonstrating how parallel multi-fidelity simulation can be used to accelerate simulation from a whole-heart model. However, the number of simulations was required to increase super-exponentially in $d$, the number of tolerance parameters appearing in the numerical method. This paper develops a refined notion of ‘extrapolation dimension’, drastically reducing this simulation requirement when multiple tolerance parameters feature in the numerical method. Sparsity-exploiting methodology is developed that is simultaneously simpler and more powerful compared to earlier work, and this is accompanied by sharp theoretical guarantees and substantial empirical support.

entry.title: Sparse Network Inference under Imperfect Detection and its Application to Ecological Networks

link.title: Sparse Network Inference under Imperfect Detection and its Application to Ecological Networks

entry.content: Recovering latent structure from count data has received considerable attention in network inference, particularly when one seeks both cross-group interactions and within-group similarity patterns in bipartite networks, which are widely used in ecology research. Such networks are often sparse and prone to imperfect detection. Existing models mainly focus on interaction recovery, while the induced similarity graphs are much less studied. Moreover, existing models for under-counted data place sparsity, if at all, on the detection model rather than on these graphs. To address these issues, we propose a nonnegative low-rank factorization framework that jointly estimates detection probabilities and promotes sparse within- and cross-group graphs through $\ell_{1/2}$ regularization. For the resulting nonconvex, nonsmooth problem, we develop an ADMM-based algorithm with adaptive penalization, and establish asymptotic feasibility and KKT stationarity of cluster points under stated assumptions. We also give sufficient conditions for exact recovery of within- and cross-group graphs. On synthetic data with up to 20% missing entries, the method recovers the graphs and detection probabilities with competitive accuracy. Across three ecological datasets, it matches the baseline held-out predictions while estimating detection probabilities and within- and cross-group graphs.

entry.title: Hypergraph Generation via Structured Stochastic Diffusion

link.title: Hypergraph Generation via Structured Stochastic Diffusion

entry.content: Hypergraphs model higher-order interactions, but realistic hypergraph generation remains difficult because incidence, hyperedge-size heterogeneity, and overlap structure are not faithfully captured by pairwise reductions. We propose \HEDGE, a generative model defined directly on relaxed incidence matrices via a structured stochastic diffusion. The forward process combines a hypergraph-specific two-sided heat operator with an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck component, preserving structure-aware noising near the data while yielding an explicit Gaussian terminal law. Conditional on an observed hypergraph, this forward process is linear-Gaussian, so conditional means, covariances, scores, and reverse-drift targets are available in closed form. We therefore learn a permutation-equivariant state-only reverse-drift field in incidence space by regressing onto exact conditional targets, and generate samples by simulating a learned reverse-time SDE from the Gaussian base law. We establish exactness in the ideal state-only setting together with finite-horizon stability guarantees, and empirically show improved hypergraph generation quality relative to strong baselines.

entry.title: NeuroMAS: Multi-Agent Systems as Neural Networks with Joint Reinforcement Learning

link.title: NeuroMAS: Multi-Agent Systems as Neural Networks with Joint Reinforcement Learning

entry.content: Multi-agent language systems are often built as hand-designed workflows, where agents are assigned semantic roles and communication protocols are specified in advance. We propose NeuroMAS, a framework that treats a multi-agent language system as a trainable and scalable neural-network-like architecture with hidden textual intermediate signals. In NeuroMAS, language-agent nodes are role-free but structure-aware: the topology determines how information can flow, while reward-based training determines how nodes communicate, specialize, and coordinate. This formulation shifts multi-agent design from workflow engineering toward architecture design, where depth, width, connectivity, and growth protocol become scalable sources of capability. We provide a theoretical perspective showing why such modular text-valued computation can be parameter-efficient when tasks admit stable decompositions. Experiments show that NeuroMAS improves over both inference-time collaboration methods and trained baselines, and that its gains are not explained by trainable parameter count alone. We further find that organizational scaling is path-dependent: larger systems can fail when trained from scratch, but become stronger when grown progressively from smaller trained systems. These results suggest that learned multi-agent organization is a promising scaling axis for language-model reasoning and generation.

entry.title: Self-Distillation is Optimal Among Spectral Shrinkage Estimators

link.title: Self-Distillation is Optimal Among Spectral Shrinkage Estimators

entry.content: Self-distillation has emerged as a promising technique for improving model performance in modern machine learning systems. We develop the statistical foundations of self-distillation in high-dimensional linear regression by introducing and analyzing a broad class of estimators, namely spectral shrinkage estimators. We consider both spiked and general covariance matrices. For the former, we establish that when the covariance has $s$ distinct spikes, $s$-step self-distillation achieves optimal prediction among spectral shrinkage estimators, outperforming well-known estimators in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, we show that $s$ steps are necessary for optimality: any $(s-k)$-step distilled estimator is strictly suboptimal for $1 \leq k \leq s$. For general covariance matrices, we show that self-distillation approaches the optimal limiting prediction risk among continuous spectral shrinkage estimators as the number of distillation steps increases. We further develop a generalized cross-validation procedure for selecting the distillation parameters from data and establish an asymptotic oracle guarantee for the resulting estimator. We also study a federated approach where multiple data centers share spectral shrinkage estimators and a common server seeks to aggregate them to achieve optimal performance. In this case, we find that the best local rule again takes the form of self-distillation, though it differs from the optimal rule when data are hosted centrally on a single server. Together, our results explain why self-distillation improves predictive performance and provide a broader statistical framework that connects it to classical shrinkage-based methods.

entry.title: Robust Ensemble Kalman Filtering Under Observation Noise Misspecification

link.title: Robust Ensemble Kalman Filtering Under Observation Noise Misspecification

entry.content: We address observation noise misspecification in Bayesian filtering of dynamical systems via generalised Bayesian inference. Mismatch in tail decay between the true data generating process and an assumed observation model, often indicated via outliers, can strongly impact Bayesian updates in Kalman filters and their ensemble approximations. Adjusting information processing in the analysis step by employing diffusion score matching achieves robustness while maintaining closed-form Gaussian updates and good uncertainty quantification. We provide theoretical properties of this novel Kalman filter in linear Gaussian state space systems covering conjugacy of the analysis step, robustness, covariance stability, and tuning. We extend the approach to non-linear signal dynamics by adapting ensemble Kalman filter variants. Simulation studies on 2D target tracking and the Lorenz-63 and 40D Lorenz-96 systems highlight a critical trade-off between robustness and stability in filtering.

entry.title: Smooth Concordance Metrics for Survival Models

link.title: Smooth Concordance Metrics for Survival Models

entry.content: Concordance indices are widely popular metrics for assessing the ability of predictive survival models to discriminate underlying risk levels. However, these statistics have also been criticized for using only the rank orderings of the model’s predicted risk scores and being insensitive to important model features, such as the addition of strong predictor variables into the model. In this paper, we address these limitations by developing smooth concordance metrics that model the underlying risk discrimination probabilities as continuous functions of the predicted risk score differences, where the shapes of these functions are estimated from the observed data. As a result, these smooth concordance metrics assess model performance across the entire range of possible risk score differences, allowing one to identify specific scenarios where the candidate model performs especially well or better than other models. Simulations show that the proposed smooth concordance metrics provide more detailed information about risk discrimination performance and are much more sensitive to the addition of meaningful predictors. We apply these methods to compare predictive survival models for cancer recurrence.

entry.title: What is the Long-Term Value of Reliability?

link.title: What is the Long-Term Value of Reliability?

entry.content: We describe Chronos LTV, a system to measure the long-term impact of delays and other service defects on key business metrics. We use Markov decision processes to model customer interactions over time, and formalize our target estimand as the marginal policy effect with respect to moving the average delay rate. Given this setup, we show that we can identify long-term effects under a sequential unconfoundedness assumption where delays are as good as random given observed order characteristics; and can estimate these effects using a simple covariate-balancing algorithm.

entry.title: Anchors Away: Navigating Single-Arm Indirect Comparisons with Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression (ML-UMR-SA)

link.title: Anchors Away: Navigating Single-Arm Indirect Comparisons with Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression (ML-UMR-SA)

entry.content: Unanchored indirect treatment comparisons using single-arm evidence are increasingly used in health technology assessment (HTA) when anchored comparisons of randomized evidence are not possible. Existing population-adjusted methods, including matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) and simulated treatment comparison (STC), are generally limited to pairwise analyses and typically estimate marginal effects in the comparator study population, which may differ from the decision-relevant target population. We propose multilevel unanchored meta-regression for single-arm indirect comparisons (ML-UMR-SA), a Bayesian outcome-regression framework for synthesizing individual patient data and aggregate data from single-arm evidence. ML-UMR-SA respecifies multilevel network meta-regression to pool absolute outcomes rather than relative treatment effects, jointly modeling individual- and aggregate-level data and linking aggregate outcomes through marginalization over study-specific covariate distributions, enabling estimation across multiple treatments, studies, and target populations. ML-UMR-SA distinguishes assumptions required to identify treatment effects from those required to transport results to target populations. Valid inference relies on strong and often unverifiable assumptions, particularly conditional constancy of absolute effects and cross-treatment identifying assumptions such as the shared prognostic factor assumption (SPFA). These requirements are made explicit within a Bayesian modeling framework that facilitates sensitivity analyses. In simulations without unobserved confounding, ML-UMR-SA produced low bias and nominal coverage for comparator-population effects. Transportability to alternative populations depended critically on identifying assumptions, whereas incorporating subgroup information restored near-unbiased estimation and nominal coverage.

entry.title: Closed-form fractional radial links for elliptical Mahalanobis discriminant analysis

link.title: Closed-form fractional radial links for elliptical Mahalanobis discriminant analysis

entry.content: We study binary classification when the two classes are elliptical with a shared radial generator $g$. The log-likelihood ratio is then an additive function of the two squared Mahalanobis radii, with radial link $\varphi=\log g$. For Gaussian classes $\varphi$ is affine and the rule reduces to quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA); otherwise the Bayes link is not the identity. Instead of fitting this link with a spline smoother, we derive its family from the within-class law of the radius and estimate a finite fractional-power projection. We prove that the link is identifiable from the radius law, that the plug-in estimator is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and asymptotically normal under finite-moment conditions, and that the induced classifier is asymptotically Bayes-optimal in an iterated sieve limit. For $d\ge2$ and non-nested class parameters, the identity link suffices only for affine (Gaussian) generators. The bridge, GAM membership and the affine direction of this dichotomy are verified in Lean 4. We compare against the global Mahalanobis-GAM of Ghosh et al. (2025), re-implemented with mgcv REML splines at equal input budget. On two UCI benchmarks the derived link ties with the fitted GAM. On six financial series from three asset classes, with validation that respects temporal dependence, it is never significantly worse than the fitted GAM: better on CAD/USD and tied on the other five. It beats QDA on the three heaviest-tailed series (oil $[+0.023,+0.069]$, S&P 500 $[+0.039,+0.125]$, JPY/USD $[+0.009,+0.047]$) and ties elsewhere. A rate simulation with a closed-form ground truth reproduces the $\sqrt{n}$ rate and, under covariance heterogeneity, QDA’s risk floor against the derived link’s vanishing excess risk. The derived link thus matches a tuned GAM without smoothing-parameter selection and improves on QDA where the generator departs from the Gaussian.

entry.title: AuditLock: Pre-Specified Verification Audits for Synthetic Tabular Data Releases

link.title: AuditLock: Pre-Specified Verification Audits for Synthetic Tabular Data Releases

entry.content: A statistical office with a synthetic version of a protected file must decide whether it may be released for a stated purpose. We study the locked audit, a pre-specified and simultaneous form of the verification servers used in official statistics. Before a protected audit sample is opened, the custodian fixes the use, the candidates, the analyses, a tolerance for each and the schedule. The audit then reports simultaneous finite-sample bounds on paired loss gaps, and a declared negative control must fail. We correct an anytime-valid sequence that an earlier release had implemented with a variance penalty four times too small. Two confirmatory rounds were pre-specified in a hash-locked local ledger and publicly timestamped only after the audits. The control and ideal-generator outcomes were near-certain by design. A Gaussian copula certified in every cell, but only inside the rounding step of the tolerance rule. A second transparent candidate certified once, against a written prediction. Learned models, at library defaults and 4,000 training rows, certified in one of 18 fits in round 1 and in none of 12 tables in round 2. The paper is a protocol and an evidence record, not a claim that any generator is private or deployable.

entry.title: Guidance for Prior Change via Density Ratio Estimation

link.title: Guidance for Prior Change via Density Ratio Estimation

entry.content: Simulation-Based Inference (SBI) serves as a vital framework for parameter inference in scientific fields where simulators involve intractable likelihoods, yet while amortized generative models offer rapid posterior estimation, they are often restricted by the specific priors used during training, thereby limiting their flexibility as prior knowledge evolves. To address this prior dependency, PriorGuide was introduced as an inference-time guidance method, but due to its intractable formulation, it relies on Gaussian approximations of the reverse transition kernel and Gaussian mixture model fitting for the prior ratio, both of which introduce systematic bias. Motivated by these limitations, we propose an unbiased test-time guidance framework that leverages Density Ratio Estimation (DRE) to learn a score guidance term, effectively decoupling the inference process from the prior training. Moreover, our framework remains agnostic to the specific density ratio estimators, making it a general and flexible framework for handling prior changes. Experimental results across multiple tasks demonstrate that our method matches or outperforms PriorGuide on C2ST and MMD in most tasks while maintaining robustness even under limited overlap between the training and target priors. Furthermore, we apply our method to Bayesian updating for parameter inference from planetary light-curve data, where it also demonstrates strong effectiveness and robustness. Code is available at https://github.com/a-chenchen/dre-based-prior-guidance .

entry.title: Response-guided knockoffs for prespecified directional FDR control in linear models

link.title: Response-guided knockoffs for prespecified directional FDR control in linear models

entry.content: Conventional false discovery rate (FDR) control limits the expected proportion of selected features that are unrelated to the response. Directional FDR extends this criterion to also account for incorrect sign estimates. In some applications, however, discoveries are sought only in a direction specified in advance. We therefore introduce the prespecified directional FDR, which counts as errors both null effects and effects opposite to the target direction in context of the fixed-design Gaussian linear model with unknown noise variance. A straightforward adaptation of the knockoff filter provides prespecified directional FDR control. To improve power, we develop the response-guided knockoff filter, which uses a noise-perturbed response to guide knockoff construction in favour of features likely to have the target sign, while retaining finite-sample prespecified directional FDR control. entry.title: Robust and Sparse Group Dynamic Causal Modeling via Student-t Parametric Empirical Bayes and Nonlocal Priors

link.title: Robust and Sparse Group Dynamic Causal Modeling via Student-t Parametric Empirical Bayes and Nonlocal Priors

entry.content: Dynamic causal modeling (DCM) estimates directed effective connectivity, while parametric empirical Bayes (PEB) supports group inference using subject-specific posterior summaries. entry.title: CleanScore: Black-Box Benchmark Audits with Negative Controls and Sensitivity Bounds

link.title: CleanScore: Black-Box Benchmark Audits with Negative Controls and Sensitivity Bounds

entry.content: Public benchmark scores reflect skill, prior exposure to the questions, or both, and for most models the training data are unknown. CleanScore is a black-box audit: the estimator needs only a correct-or-incorrect score for each form, not training data or weights. Each benchmark question becomes a parent item with one public form and two independently written fresh forms that keep its numbers, facts and answer. The audit reports an interval for the public-form advantage, not a verdict, and a private control bank with an explicit transport radius provides a proxy for the ordinary form gap that a rewrite alone can produce. A registered controlled-exposure experiment, a preliminary validation, detects planted exposure in one of two model families. A registered audit of five open models on 200 GSM8K and 200 ARC-Challenge items (ARC with stem-only rewrites, scored by option log probabilities) finds no exposure-consistent advantage, and two reruns declared before they were run (GSM8K at a longer token budget, ARC scored from generated letters) leave that conclusion unchanged. For four of the ten model-benchmark pairs the upper end of the interval is about five points or less, and for none is it above 21 points. The registered claim rule is much less sensitive than the primary interval: it flags a planted ten-point advantage in 5% to 11% of audits. Registered positive controls show what a null can mean. In four models, each trained under four seeds, items leaked into fine-tuning gained 25 points on average over unleaked items on the leaked wording and 19 points on paraphrases the model never saw, so a substantial share of the effect, estimated at 76% (95% interval 50% to 113%), is invisible to a paraphrase audit. A null on surface form says much less about contamination than the name suggests.

entry.title: Calibrated Order-Randomized Rosenblatt Tests

link.title: Calibrated Order-Randomized Rosenblatt Tests

entry.content: We test whether a multivariate vector X conforms to a specified distribution F, as in copula modelling and density forecasting. The Rosenblatt transform reduces this to testing uniformity, but its arbitrary coordinate ordering affects power under dependence. We study order randomization: transforming under many random orderings and merging evidence with dependence-robust rules. Reordering only redistributes the Mahalanobis signal energy, so one ordering is a lucky or unlucky draw, and pooling raises calibrated power. We compare against two order-invariant baselines, the chi-squared energy test and the symmetric-root test. With F known, the e-value average over orderings is at least as powerful as the symmetric-root test in every setting we ran, and as the chi-squared test on concentrated and fully diffuse departures. With Gaussian mean and covariance estimated, the classical conditional probability integral transform keeps each ordering’s p-values exact and e-values valid, a parametric bootstrap calibrates the pooled tests, and the comparisons hold except for deficits of at most 0.02 against the symmetric-root test on single-coordinate departures. Validating a Gaussian risk model for nine currencies, the test flags Brexit, COVID and other episodes; it extends to any null with computable, simulable conditionals.

entry.title: Hurricane recovery gaps lie in reconnection, not local restart

link.title: Hurricane recovery gaps lie in reconnection, not local restart

entry.content: Climate-intensified hurricanes disrupt urban mobility, yet whether recovery is equitable across the rural-urban gradient is unclear. Analyzing device-based mobility for Hurricanes Helene and Milton, we find local activity restarted within approximately 4.5 days in both storms, whereas reconnection to the outside world took 5 days in coastal-urban Florida but 11 in inland-rural Appalachia. The gap lies in external reconnection, not local restart, implying planners should target rural isolation.

entry.title: Covariance-Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference

link.title: Covariance-Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference

entry.content: In prediction-powered inference, predictions supplement labeled outcomes to improve estimation. We combine a prediction-corrected score and an auxiliary moment in a generalized method of moments (GMM) criterion. The resulting estimator is first-order equivalent to the corresponding corrected-score root under regularity conditions, but the auxiliary penalty can change the finite-sample fit. In a multiparameter Gaussian linear model with low noise, retaining this penalty reduces risk relative to bounded scalar corrected-score roots. We then introduce covariance-calibrated prediction-powered inference (CC-PPI), which uses prediction scores from both samples to reweight the penalty. With a spectrally protected half-strength update, CC-PPI retains regular first-order efficiency and strictly reduces risk relative to uncalibrated full GMM in a Gaussian linear low-noise regime that tolerates some prediction error and in a structured multiparameter logistic model conditional on the existence of a finite pilot estimate. Targeted simulations isolate the gains from calibration and show that they can reverse as prediction error grows. Broader simulations and four applications evaluate point estimation and the coverage and width of full-refit bootstrap intervals for linear projections.

entry.title: FasterRW: An Efficient Prior-Assisted Random Walk Solver for Thermal Analysis

link.title: FasterRW: An Efficient Prior-Assisted Random Walk Solver for Thermal Analysis

entry.content: Thermal simulation is becoming increasingly critical in modern IC design and manufacturing. Feynman–Kac random walk methods can estimate localized temperatures without solving the global field, but in practical settings without Dirichlet boundaries they require very long paths to control the truncation residual. This paper presents FasterRW, a continuation-value framework for accelerating Feynman–Kac thermal random walks. We prove a stopping-time residual identity showing that the expected tail after truncation equals the current attenuation weight multiplied by the temperature at the stopping location. This identity enables a prior-corrected single-point estimator: a cheap, noisy prior replaces the unknown continuation value, making the truncation bias scale with prior error rather than absolute temperature and yielding an error-controlled threshold-selection rule. For multi-point queries, FasterRW further converts cross-query pass-through tails into pseudo-samples and refines the resulting observations in prior-error coordinates through kriging. Compared with prior state-of-the-art methods, FasterRW achieves up to $28\times$ acceleration while maintaining accuracy. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/ShiningSord/FastRW.

entry.title: Wrap or Rewrite? Reviving the 1989 GlobalMinimum Bayesian Global-Optimization Library for R and Python

link.title: Wrap or Rewrite? Reviving the 1989 GlobalMinimum Bayesian Global-Optimization Library for R and Python

entry.content: The GlobalMinimum library of Jonas Mockus (1989) implements some of the earliest practical Bayesian global-optimization methods – one-step Bayesian search over a simple surrogate, Wiener-process one-dimensional models, low-discrepancy designs, and clustering multistart. We modernize this Fortran 66/77 codebase along both standard routes: wrapping the original compiled routines behind R and Python packages, and translating the core methods to Rust. First, we release packages in which every optimizer runs the genuine 1989 algorithms, with callback objectives, deterministic seeding, full evaluation traces, and validation that retrofits memory- and I/O-safety onto COMMON-block Fortran. Second, we dissect a translation-fidelity incident: the Rust port of the one-step Bayesian planner ran up to 12x slower than the wrapped Fortran – initially misattributed to foreign-function overhead. Controlled decomposition shows call overhead is microseconds and backend-neutral; the cause was two dropped pruning rules whose restoration recovers bitwise trajectory agreement and speed parity. The same audit found transposed coefficient matrices in re-implemented Shekel and Hartmann test functions – quiet correctness bugs of the rewrite route. Third, we benchmark the 1989 methods against modern optimizers in both ecosystems (SciPy, NLopt, CMA-ES, GP-based Bayesian optimization, GenSA, DEoptim, GA) on a COCO-style shifted-instance suite with external validation on BBOB. On classical test functions the coordinate Wiener-model search EXKOR statistically ties dual annealing at the larger budget; on BBOB’s non-separable, ill-conditioned functions it drops to mid-field, quantifying the separability dependence. At tight budgets modern annealing and GP expected improvement dominate the 1989 machinery. Code and data are available.

entry.title: Electoral Intelligence: A Neural Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial Model for Forecasting Swedish Municipal Elections

link.title: Electoral Intelligence: A Neural Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial Model for Forecasting Swedish Municipal Elections

entry.content: Forecasting local elections is difficult because electoral competition is geographically heterogeneous, highly overdispersed, and characterized by many party-municipality combinations with little or no electoral activity. This article develops a bounded neural zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) model for forecasting party-level vote counts in Swedish municipal elections. The model combines a count component for expected votes, a zero-inflation component for structural electoral absence, municipality-specific dispersion, and learned embeddings capturing latent party, municipality, and party-municipality structure. Model training relies on data from the 2014, 2018, and 2022 Swedish municipal elections and performance is evaluated on a held-out set of municipalities. Testing results show strong predictive accuracy in both vote counts and vote shares. Explanatory diagnostics indicate that latent party structure, local party-municipality relationships, electoral persistence, organizational capacity, and candidate-electorate representational similarity are among the most important determinants of predictive performance. Following model evaluation and diagnostics, the selected specification is refit on all historical data and applied to generate forecasts for the 2026 municipal elections. The proposed framework provides a flexible approach for studying local electoral competition in multiparty systems characterized by heterogeneous party presence and substantial geographic variation.

entry.title: Online and Survey Representations of Well-Being: Coherence and Cross-Source Correspondence

link.title: Online and Survey Representations of Well-Being: Coherence and Cross-Source Correspondence

entry.content: Digital traces may complement population surveys in the measurement of well-being, but the two sources do not necessarily capture identical constructs. We compare the Human Flourishing Geographic Index (HFGI) with World Values Survey and European Social Survey measures across three domains using structural equation models. The results show strong within-source coherence and construct-specific cross-source correspondence. Cross-source convergence varies across domains; the observed pattern is consistent with stronger correspondence where the underlying indicators are more closely aligned conceptually. Near-perfect agreement would be unexpected, since surveys elicit standardized self-reports, whereas HFGI captures naturally occurring public expressions. HFGI should therefore be viewed as a distinct but empirically connected measurement system that complements survey-based evidence on well-being.

entry.title: ELPAC: Endpoint-Anchored Latent Progression with Stage-Varying Multimodal Coordination

link.title: ELPAC: Endpoint-Anchored Latent Progression with Stage-Varying Multimodal Coordination

entry.content: Aging cohorts increasingly combine imaging, plasma, and cognitive measurements, but most subjects provide only a partially observed cross-sectional snapshot, leaving latent stage, progression subtype, and stage-varying multimodal coordination to be inferred jointly. Existing methods estimate the cohort-level aging process, model covariance under observed covariates, or fuse modalities for prediction. However, they rarely target the joint problem of endpoint-anchored staging and progression-resolved residual coordination across modalities, even though subject staging, subtype assignment, and multimodal interplay are mutually dependent. We introduce ELPAC, a Bayesian framework with two interlocking constructions. The first integrates subtype trajectories backward from clinically reliable endpoint groups along biologically structured velocity components encoding modality-specific monotone direction and optional sequential ordering priors. The second factorizes residual multimodal variation around the inferred stage axis into sparse coordination axes whose loadings and activations expose which multimodal patterns are operative in each subtype and when they emerge, with stage-resolved variation supplying the auxiliary structure for conditional identifiability. We use a scalable amortized variational inference scheme that enables joint posterior inference at cohort scale with single-pass deployment on new subjects. On synthetic data and a harmonized ADNI+NACC/SCAN Alzheimer’s cohort, ELPAC demonstrates accurate latent-structure recovery, well-calibrated prediction intervals, and biologically interpretable multimodal coordination programs that differ by subtype.

entry.title: Minimax designs and estimators for causal inference under network interference

link.title: Minimax designs and estimators for causal inference under network interference

entry.content: We develop a design-based minimax theory for linear causal estimands under interference. We study the minimax risks of three problems: optimizing an estimator under a fixed design, optimizing an estimator and a design from a restricted class, or optimizing both over all designs. In each problem, we study the minimax risk over all estimators and over design-unbiased estimators separately. We allow any correctly specified exposure mapping, including the identity. Our theory represents causal inference under interference as a constrained sampling design on an expanded finite population of $\sum_i d_i$ potential outcomes, where $d_i$ is the number of exposure levels attainable by unit $i$. We describe the constrained sampling design by a weighted sampling hypergraph: its vertices are the potential outcomes, its hyperedges are the maximal sets of potential outcomes that can be jointly sampled under feasible treatment assignments, and its weights are induced by the randomization design. We show that the minimax risks of the fixed-design, restricted-design, and all-design problems depend, respectively, on the weighted hypergraph induced by the design, the collection of weighted hypergraphs attainable within the restricted class, and the unweighted hypergraph. Our Bayes lower bounds compare potential-outcome tables that differ on jointly missing sets of potential outcomes: joint-missingness probabilities govern the lower bounds over all estimators, whereas the corresponding odds govern the lower bounds over unbiased estimators. We illustrate the theory for average treatment effects without interference, saturation designs under partial interference, total, direct, and contagion effects under neighborhood interference, and bipartite dose-response contrasts. The upper and lower bounds match in several settings.

entry.title: A tractable transition function for the Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection via gamma duality

link.title: A tractable transition function for the Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection via gamma duality

entry.content: The transition function of the Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection is a fundamental object for non-neutral evolutionary modelling and likelihood-based inference, but, unlike in the neutral case, existing representations are impractical or inefficient. Spectral approaches rely on truncation levels that grow with selection strength and the number of alleles, thus leading to rapidly increasing computational costs, while existing duality-based expansions lead to multi-type dual processes whose transition probabilities involve intractable normalising constants. In this paper we obtain a new transition-function representation for the multi-allelic Wright-Fisher diffusion with parent-independent mutation and genic selection that makes transition-law evaluation and simulation practically feasible in regimes where existing methods are costly or unavailable. The key tool is a new gamma duality, obtained by augmenting classical polynomial duality by an exponential tilting and yields a multivariate birth-death dual with fully explicit infinitesimal rates and an entrance-boundary construction. This is used to express the Wright-Fisher transition law as an explicit mixture of standard Dirichlet components, with mixing weights obtained from the dual started from its entrance boundary. We characterise the dual stationary distribution and its small-time behaviour, and develop practical and efficient sampling procedures for both transition and stationary laws, including a fast approximate stationary sampler with explicit error control. Numerical experiments illustrate substantial runtime gains over specialised methods in regimes where they apply, while our approach remains applicable for arbitrary numbers of alleles and selection coefficients.

entry.title: False Discovery Rate Control via Prediction-Based, Model-Agnostic Data Splitting: An Application to Gut Microbiome Data in Liver Function

link.title: False Discovery Rate Control via Prediction-Based, Model-Agnostic Data Splitting: An Application to Gut Microbiome Data in Liver Function

entry.content: Many methods have been proposed to control the false discovery rate (FDR) in feature selection, yet challenges remain when the relationship between predictors and the outcome is complex. We propose a prediction-based data-splitting procedure that can leverage flexible predictive models while controlling the FDR. The data are divided into three parts: one for model training and two for constructing the mirror statistic. For each feature, we construct a negative control using the remaining features without incorporating outcome information and define a test statistic based on the resulting change in predictive performance. Under the null, such a perturbation is approximately equally likely to increase or decrease predictive performance, yielding a statistic symmetric about zero. In contrast, perturbing an informative feature tends to reduce predictive performance, resulting in a large positive statistic. Features are selected by thresholding these statistics, with false discoveries estimated from the corresponding negative tail to control the FDR. We apply the proposed method to liver function microbiome data, where high-dimensional, correlated features and potentially complex feature–outcome relationships make reliable type I error control particularly important for reproducible scientific discovery. Through simulation studies and the real-data application, we demonstrate that the proposed framework provides robust FDR control and can be integrated with state-of-the-art machine-learning models to accommodate complex relationships between features and the outcome.

entry.title: Dynamic Smart Charging Through Integrated Agent-based Simulation and Optimization Modeling

link.title: Dynamic Smart Charging Through Integrated Agent-based Simulation and Optimization Modeling

entry.content: Coordinated electric vehicle (EV) charging can improve alignment between transportation operations and power-system conditions as electrification expands. This study develops an integrated simulation-optimization framework that embeds demand-aware charging (DAC) and grid-responsive charging, including unidirectional smart charging (V1G) and vehicle-to-grid (V2G), within an agent-based model, enabling dynamic feedback between optimized vehicle (dis)charging decisions and evolving transportation-system states. Using the Austin 6-county region, the framework evaluates 15,000 shared autonomous electric vehicles (SAEVs) under DAC, V1G, fleet-only V2G, and combined fleet-plus-household V2G. Results show coordinated strategies concentrate charging toward midday and provide selective evening discharge while maintaining service performance. Under favorable pricing, V2G reduces net CO2 emissions from 45 kg/SAEV/day under DAC to below 40 kg and lowers emission intensity by up to 14% to 0.14 kg per vehicle-mile traveled. DAC and V1G offer near-term options, whereas high V2G costs may hinder adoption. Realized benefits depend on tariffs, vehicle availability, and V2G maturity.

entry.title: Blind Noise Equalization for Large Data Matrices under General Variance Profiles

link.title: Blind Noise Equalization for Large Data Matrices under General Variance Profiles

entry.content: Low-rank approximation is a basic tool for inference from large and noisy data matrices. However, when noise variances differ across entries, a setting known as heteroskedasticity, the noise can distort the observed spectrum, producing spurious components and obscuring weak signals. To address these challenges, we develop BRINE (Blind Resolvent-based Iterative Noise Equalizer), a data-driven procedure that iteratively rescales rows and columns to equalize the average noise variance across both dimensions. Under suitable conditions, this procedure restores the Marchenko-Pastur law for the noise spectrum and can amplify signal components without prior knowledge of the signal or noise structure. A key idea underlying our approach is to equalize the diagonal entries of the data resolvent as a proxy for equalizing the unknown noise variances. At the population level, we identify a potential function that characterizes this equalization and motivates an iterative minimization procedure. We prove convergence of the iterations to the true equalizer for arbitrary positive variance profiles, with a geometric rate under mild conditions. The updates can be estimated directly from noisy data, and we establish probabilistic error bounds for the scaling factors. Simulations and experiments across diverse biological data modalities and preprocessing pipelines illustrate the effectiveness of our approach.

entry.title: Beyond the Lower-Star Filtration: Alternative Filtration Methods for Persistent Homology

link.title: Beyond the Lower-Star Filtration: Alternative Filtration Methods for Persistent Homology

entry.content: In the lower-star filtration (LSF), simplices are assigned filtration values according to the maximum-vertex rule, with each simplex entering the filtration when its highest-valued vertex appears. A limitation of this construction is that some higher-dimensional simplices may enter simultaneously with their boundary faces, causing certain topological features to be filled immediately upon formation and thus not appear in the resulting persistence diagram. To address this limitation, we propose three alternative filtration methods: the (\varepsilon)-lower-star filtration (ELSF), the (L_p) filtration (LpF), and the softmax filtration (SMF). {ELSF introduces a dimension-dependent delay to the maximum-vertex rule,} allowing higher-dimensional simplices to enter the filtration after their boundary faces, whereas {LpF and SMF use aggregation functions that depend on all vertex values rather} than solely on their maximum. By modifying how filtration values are assigned, these methods allow simplices to enter the filtration more progressively, so that topological features such as loops and voids may persist over longer filtration intervals rather than being filled immediately. Consequently, the resulting persistence diagrams may include persistence features that are not observed under LSF, potentially providing useful information for distinguishing data populations. Experimental results on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed filtration methods are computationally efficient and can provide greater sensitivity to structural differences in the data than LSF.

entry.title: Bayesian Unit-level Quantile Modeling with Application to Wealth Data

link.title: Bayesian Unit-level Quantile Modeling with Application to Wealth Data

entry.content: Modeling wealth quantiles over time and space and across fine-grained demographic classifications is of vital importance to policy makers. However, such data present unique challenges for standard small area estimation methodologies because they are highly skewed and heavy-tailed with both positive and negative values. Traditional area-level modeling and design-based approaches struggle to capture these features. Meanwhile, existing unit-level methodology frequently treats the survey design as ignorable and does not apply to surveys that are repeated over time. Often the analysis is restricted to alternative response variables that are non-negative, such as poverty indicators or income. To overcome these limitations, we propose a Bayesian, asymmetric Laplace pseudolikelihood model that is able to capture the major features of wealth while adjusting for survey weights and accounting for both spatial and temporal dependence. We present a Gibbs sampling algorithm for our model, as well as a variational Bayes algorithm for fast computation. We apply the method to the Survey of Income and Program Participation to characterize geographic, temporal, and demographic variation in the distribution of U.S. household wealth, including for sparsely sampled domains where direct estimates are unavailable or unstable.

entry.title: Competitive Balance Beyond Standings: Bayesian Inference for Latent Tiers and Structural Heterogeneity

link.title: Competitive Balance Beyond Standings: Bayesian Inference for Latent Tiers and Structural Heterogeneity

entry.content: Competitive balance has long been a central concern in sports economics, tied to outcome uncertainty, fan engagement, and the way leagues design their policies. Most existing measures of competitive balance are built from standings or winning percentages, which say little about how overall parity relates to the way teams sort into latent competitive tiers. We propose a Bayesian framework based on the Bradley-Terry model that jointly estimates the number of competitive tiers and team memberships. To capture the overall degree of competitive heterogeneity, we introduce a structural balance parameter defined on the unit interval within a hierarchical model, and we establish theoretical results giving this parameter a clear interpretation:it is directly tied to the separation between tiers, and overall heterogeneity depends on both the size and frequency of cross-tier differences. Importantly, structural balance is distinct from the information content of the schedule itself, so leagues with different numbers of teams and games can be compared on equal footing. Inference is carried out with an efficient posterior sampling algorithm that jointly handles team abilities, tier structure, home advantage, and structural balance. Simulation studies validate the proposed method, showing accurate recovery of the latent competitive structure and correct performance of the structural-balance testing procedure. Applied to the NBA and NFL, it reveals that the two leagues exhibit similar global structural balance despite very different competitive organizations: the NBA has three latent tiers, while the NFL has two broader ones, and the NFL’s sparser schedule produces considerably more posterior uncertainty. Overall parity, it turns out, can mask quite different forms of competitive stratification-something standings-based measures alone cannot detect.

entry.title: Snow Changes Drought Characterization but Not Drought Predictability: A Leakage-Free Multiscale Study in Ohio

link.title: Snow Changes Drought Characterization but Not Drought Predictability: A Leakage-Free Multiscale Study in Ohio

entry.content: We examine whether accounting for snow accumulation and melt, which precipitation-based drought indices ignore, changes drought characterization and one-month-ahead drought forecasting at three stations in Ohio, USA (1953–2026). The Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) is compared with the Standardized Snow Melt and Rain Index (SMRI), and both are decomposed with the Haar maximal overlap discrete wavelet transform. Nonlinear autoregressive networks without (NAR) and with (NARX) wavelet inputs are compared over 100 paired repetitions in a leakage-free design (past-only wavelet inputs, untouched test period), together with persistence, climatology, and linear autoregressive benchmarks. Snow changes the 3-month index mainly from December to May (mean absolute SMRI–SPI differences of up to 0.17–0.28). These differences are attributable to the snow-adjusted input rather than to the fitted distribution, are robust to the snow-model parameters, and change the drought classification of 21–32\% of the December–May drought months. Wavelet inputs reduce NARX error relative to NAR by 6–10\% for the 3-month indices in 92–100\% of the repetitions, but not for the 6-month indices. A linear autoregression with 7–12 lags is at least as accurate as two-lag NARX for every series, and networks given six lags gain at most 4.5\% from the wavelet inputs and only match the autoregression. The forecast gain therefore reflects the memory of the accumulated index rather than multiscale information, and it is similar for the SPI and the SMRI. Snow matters for drought monitoring in winter and spring, but not for one-month predictability.

entry.title: Advection-aligned block Vecchia inference for spatio-temporal Gaussian processes

link.title: Advection-aligned block Vecchia inference for spatio-temporal Gaussian processes

entry.content: Vecchia approximations enable scalable likelihood-based inference for large Gaussian process models, but their accuracy depends on the choice of conditioning sets. For spatio-temporal processes with advection, target-centered conditioning can omit informative past observations. Motivated by total column ozone observations from the Geostationary Environment Monitoring Spectrometer (GEMS), we propose a data-driven, advection-aligned block Vecchia approximation that incorporates estimated transport direction into temporal conditioning geometry. Observation locations need not lie on a regular grid. An initial advection vector is estimated from the data and used once to select transport-aligned past-time conditioning blocks. The resulting graph is held fixed during optimization, while covariance and advection parameters remain free to vary. This separates neighbor selection from covariance estimation, avoids repeated parameter-dependent neighbor searches, and provides an interpretable connection between conditioning geometry and estimated transport. Batched graphics processing unit (GPU) operations evaluate the likelihood and its gradients. In a matched comparison of daily GEMS datasets from July 2024 and July 2025, advection-aligned conditioning attained a lower fitted Vecchia negative log-likelihood than target-centered conditioning on 53 of 61 days. In six Mat'ern simulation scenarios with 120 matched eight-hour fields each, advection-aligned conditioning reduced advection-vector root mean squared error relative to target-centered conditioning at the same conditioning-block budget, with the largest reduction under strong transport.

entry.title: Supervised Factor-Augmented Matrix Regression with Weak Factors

link.title: Supervised Factor-Augmented Matrix Regression with Weak Factors

entry.content: We develop a supervised factor-augmented matrix regression framework for high-dimensional analysis with weak factors. When factor loadings are concentrated on unknown subsets of rows and columns, conventional full-matrix factor extraction may suffer substantial signal dilution, with weakness in one matrix dimension propagating to estimation in the other. We characterize this two-way weak-loading phenomenon for both (\alpha)-PCA and projected estimators and show that their loading and factor estimates may deteriorate under weak signals. To address this problem, we propose a sequential response-guided screening procedure that identifies informative rows and columns prior to factor extraction. We establish exact support recovery and show that post-screening factor re-estimation converts the weak-loading problem into a pervasive one relative to the retained dimensions, yielding sharper convergence rates under substantially weaker dimensional growth conditions and consistent factor-number determination. We further establish asymptotic distributions for both unrestricted and bilinear regression estimators based on the estimated matrix factors. Simulations demonstrate substantial improvements in support recovery and factor estimation under weak signals. We illustrate the gains obtained by the response-guided factor construction with two empirical applications.

entry.title: Portfolio-aware scenario transfer of reserve movements: evidence from Lloyd’s syndicates

link.title: Portfolio-aware scenario transfer of reserve movements: evidence from Lloyd’s syndicates

entry.content: A claims-development movement on one portfolio may not transfer directly as a stress to another size. We estimate how to transfer such scenarios between portfolio sizes, using 632 syndicate-years from 117 Lloyd’s syndicates over 2015-2024. The measured movement is the change in gross claims estimates on selected older underwriting cohorts, divided by opening gross claims outstanding plus reserves taken on in the year whose development it includes; it is not a pure measure of opening-reserve deterioration. Its dispersion falls materially with reserve size, and a size-based scale predicts held-out syndicates far better than a single market scale. But the transferred upper tail understates the smallest books: in the smallest reserve-size quartile, six of 158 held-out observations exceeded the transferred 99.5th percentile, against 0.79 expected, from three syndicates. Square-root scaling has descriptively lower held-out pinball loss at 99% and 99.5%, though more misses among the largest books. For a GBP 500m portfolio the transferred empirical 99.5th percentile is 0.34 of reserves (95% credible interval, conditional on the fitted model, 0.23-0.52), against 0.67 in the raw market pool. Both are Syndicate 5820’s 2016 movement. The contribution is inspectable scenario comparability, not a calibrated capital quantile or a next-year forecast.
