entry.title: New optimisations for exact, scalable 2D Gaussian process inference, with applications to astronomical time-series

link.title: New optimisations for exact, scalable 2D Gaussian process inference, with applications to astronomical time-series

entry.content: Astronomical datasets often consist of a grid of datapoints in two or more dimensions, such as images, spectroscopic time-series, and imaging time-series. Gaussian processes (GPs) are a powerful tool for dealing with correlated noise in these data, arising from both astrophysical and instrumental systematics. Despite this, popular GP optimisations such as celerite are largely restricted to 1D datasets. Extensions to 2D data typically come with limited flexibility or poor scaling. As a motivating example, this limitation is significant for transiting exoplanet spectroscopy with JWST, as current analyses typically assume each spectroscopic light curve is statistically independent, despite many potential sources of wavelength-correlation, including detector readout noise and stellar granulation. This introduces a potential bias in atmospheric retrievals which is typically ignored. To solve this problem, we present new, exact GP optimisations implemented in the JAX-based package luas, which extend 1D GP optimisations to multidimensional data using Kronecker product algebra. These GP optimisations are highly flexible, permit efficient analysis of 2D datasets containing millions of datapoints, and in many cases have a cheaper cost than transit light curve modelling. These optimisations are key to pushing the limits of exoplanet spectroscopy to smaller targets around bright host stars, as we increasingly hit instrumental and astrophysical noise floors. We suggest further applications to the analysis of ground-based high resolution spectroscopic time-series, extreme precision radial velocities, and high-contrast imaging, drawing on the connection that certain 2D GP models represent a probabilistic generalisation of PCA. Applications may even extend to machine learning and geostatistics, as we present novel optimisations for the Linear Mixing Model and the Linear Model of Coregionalisation.

entry.title: Replication Certification at Publication: Checkable by Anyone, Anywhere, in Seconds, Forever

link.title: Replication Certification at Publication: Checkable by Anyone, Anywhere, in Seconds, Forever

entry.content: Authors increasingly deposit replication datasets—the data and code behind publications—in archives, and journals increasingly require them to, under progressively onerous rules. But a deposit alone proves little, so authors keep paying: months for the journal’s reanalyses, years answering readers’ questions, and rancor as failed replications become accusations because no record establishes what actually ran. We introduce a replication certificate: a cryptographically signed record of the deposited files and logged output. It replaces the journal’s reanalyses with evidence anyone can check in seconds, which no one, including the archive, can backdate, and no one can fake without risking detection. Certification asks little of anyone and benefits everyone: The author deposits, then reruns the analysis once under a random seed the archive computes from the deposit’s hash and a blockchain block; the archive signs, timestamps (in that blockchain), and stores the record—confidential data included—without rerunning anything; the journal merely checks a website for the certificate; and anyone can check or replay any step decades later.

entry.title: Power improvements and exact shortcuts for closed permutation maxT testing with discrete data

link.title: Power improvements and exact shortcuts for closed permutation maxT testing with discrete data

entry.content: In permutation tests with discrete data, especially in small samples, different permutations often yield the same test statistic. The resulting ties can make the test conservative and reduce power. This conservatism can be particularly pronounced for maximum statistics: permutations may have the same maximum but differ at other endpoints, so the remaining endpoint statistics are discarded. We develop two power improvements for closed permutation maxT tests by refining the treatment of ties. The first method uses a single uniform random variable shared across all local tests in the closed testing procedure. This shared-uniform construction maximizes the rejection probability of every elementary hypothesis among all ways of coordinating the same randomized local tests. entry.title: Causal graph fusion across incomplete cohorts and causal steering of tabular foundation models

link.title: Causal graph fusion across incomplete cohorts and causal steering of tabular foundation models

entry.content: Clinical data are split across incomplete cohorts with partially overlapping variables. Causal discovery under missing data and multi-source integration have developed separately, and tabular foundation models cannot take a causal graph without retraining. We make two contributions. First, causal graph fusion learns a partial ancestral graph on the shared variables, fuses it into each cohort’s graph under temporal background knowledge and lets Markov blankets guide re-imputation, so missing data are handled inside discovery. Second, causal attention steering compiles the learned graph into the attention of a frozen tabular foundation model at inference. Against known ground truth, fusion dominates pooled and per-cohort baselines in every missingness and heterogeneity condition tested (p<0.001), and steering improves discrimination under distribution shift (p<10^{-5}), a gain that a random graph does not produce. In two spinal cord injury cohorts, fusion orients age, albumin and hemoglobin as ancestors of length of stay, a set no single cohort orients in full, and yields compact, temporally ordered predictor sets that match or exceed automatic feature selection on four of five outcomes.

entry.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)

link.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)

entry.content: Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite this broad potential impact, selection bias is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct it, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle and assumptions, and we compare methods addressing the same form of selection by their assumptions, data requirements and limitations. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R, prepares input for the external SPREG software, and provides worked examples on simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection, one of which we present in full. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with recommendations for bias-aware study design, sensitivity analysis and reporting.

entry.title: Debias Online Expectile Regression for High-Dimensional Stream Data and Statistic Inference

link.title: Debias Online Expectile Regression for High-Dimensional Stream Data and Statistic Inference

entry.content: Expectile regression is a powerful tool for capturing heterogeneous structures in data and has attracted increasing attention in large-scale data analysis due to its computational efficiency. However, statistical inference for high-dimensional online expectile regression remains underexplored. In this paper, we propose a debiased online expectile regression method for high-dimensional streaming data. The proposed method incorporates Lasso regularization to perform variable selection and alleviate estimation instability caused by high dimensionality. It further adopts an online updating strategy in which recursively updated cumulative statistics are used to approximate the global gradient, and a proximal gradient descent algorithm is employed to update model parameters. To enable valid inference when only the current batch and historical summary statistics are available, we also develop an online precision matrix estimation procedure. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed debiased estimator. Extensive numerical studies and real-data applications show that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to the oracle and offline estimators while maintaining low storage cost.

entry.title: A hybrid model for zero-inflated proportion data

link.title: A hybrid model for zero-inflated proportion data

entry.content: This paper proposes a hybrid model for analyzing zero-inflated proportion data by distinguishing two types of zeros. The first type arises from sampling variability, whereas the second reflects intrinsically unsuitable covariates. Accordingly, the hybrid model combines a regression component for suitable observations with an estimator of the suitability region that identifies unsuitable covariates. Using a debiasing technique, we establish the consistency of both the regression and classification components, together with the asymptotic normality of the regression coefficient and a convergence rate for the support estimator. Comprehensive simulation studies verify our theoretical findings. We further apply the model to two real datasets, where it outperforms most competing methods.

entry.title: FlexRL: an R package for Flexible Record Linkage and Linked Data Quality Assessment

link.title: FlexRL: an R package for Flexible Record Linkage and Linked Data Quality Assessment

entry.content: FlexRL is an R package for probabilistic record linkage and inference on linked data. It provides a method to link observations from the same entities across two data sources that lack a unique identifier but share partially identifying variables. This method fits a hierarchical latent variable model of the data generation process, rather than classifying pairs of records from the comparison of their values, and accommodates registration errors and variables changing over time. Since linkage may affect subsequent analyses, the package also provides tools to assess the linked data quality as functions of the linkage decision rule. Two false discovery proportion estimators are implemented: a probabilistic approach contingent on the record linkage model and an augmented approach relying on an auxiliary estimation using synthetic data. Several measures of divergence of the linked sample from the source population are provided. These tools are agnostic to the underlying record linkage model and can be applied to any method. Together, they connect the output of the linkage to the validity of the subsequent analyses. The implementation combines standard R functions and S3 methods with Rcpp computations, resulting in fast execution times and a low memory footprint.

entry.title: Scalable Estimation and Inference for Varying Coefficient Expectile Regression with Streaming Data

link.title: Scalable Estimation and Inference for Varying Coefficient Expectile Regression with Streaming Data

entry.content: Nonparametric expectile regression methods face new challenges from streaming data, where retaining the full dataset for batch processing becomes increasingly impractical. In this paper, we develop a scalable nonparametric expectile regression framework for varying coefficient models. We estimate the coefficient functions online via functional stochastic gradient descent with Polyak–Ruppert averaging in a product reproducing kernel Hilbert space, requiring only gradient information and one pass over the data. For this online estimator, we establish non-asymptotic error bounds, prove its optimal nonparametric convergence rate under the proposed step-size schemes, and derive its Berry–Esseen bound for pointwise asymptotic normality. To perform online inference for the varying coefficient expectile regression models, we propose a multiplier bootstrap procedure that perturbs the stochastic gradients with independent random weights and recursively constructs bootstrap trajectories. We establish the bootstrap consistency of the online inference procedure, yielding asymptotically valid pointwise confidence intervals. Simulation studies and a real data application confirm the performance of the proposed methods.

entry.title: M-Estimation in Censored Regression Model under Endogeneity

link.title: M-Estimation in Censored Regression Model under Endogeneity

entry.content: This paper develops a general M-estimation framework for censored regression models under endogeneity. A two-stage estimation is proposed to address the issue of endogeneity in the first stage and the issue of censoring in linear regression models in the second stage. The issue of endogeneity is addressed via instrumental variables using the control function approach. The issue of censoring in linear regression models is addressed via M-estimation using a suitably defined class of loss functions yielding a class of estimators. Thus, the proposed general M-estimation framework nests several existing estimators as special cases for the respective loss functions. Moreover, this provides flexibility of accommodating a broad range of robust loss functions that have not previously been studied in the context of censored regression. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality for the proposed class of estimators. An empirical study based on simulated datasets is conducted to illustrate general M-estimation for various choices of loss functions and to examine the finite-sample performance of various resulting estimators.

entry.title: Risk-set reconstruction balance: zero-targeted diagnostics for artificial censoring in clone-censor-weight analyses

link.title: Risk-set reconstruction balance: zero-targeted diagnostics for artificial censoring in clone-censor-weight analyses

entry.content: In clone-censor-weight (CCW) analyses, inverse probability of censoring weighting corrects selection from artificial censoring at protocol deviation. Balance diagnostics, such as the end-of-grace between-strategy standardised mean difference (SMD) and censoring balance, compare different populations, and their zero targets under a correct model are not formally stated. We show that, under positivity and a correct censoring model, the weighted retained individuals reconstruct the risk set before each censoring interval and the baseline population, and we propose risk-set reconstruction balance (RRB), which measures how far they depart from these two populations. Interval RRB has a zero target for every history function, including post-baseline covariates, for which between-strategy SMDs have none. Cumulative RRB keeps a zero target for baseline covariates after outcome events, whereas the end-of-grace SMD acquires a depletion term. In simulations, interval RRB responded to an omitted term’s effect on censoring whether or not the term was prognostic. Under correct models, the exceedance rate of its studentised maximum over a null reference for chance imbalance was 3.5-6.0% (nominal 5%) when the censoring model pooled nine intervals and mostly 1.0-4.5% under censoring in a single interval. With many early events, cumulative RRB stayed near zero, whereas the end-of-grace SMD reached 0.40; under loss to follow-up that the weights ignored, cumulative RRB departed from zero and interval RRB stayed small. In a case study, interval RRB flagged a dispensing indicator outside the censoring model. Interval RRB checks the censoring model, and cumulative RRB the representation of the baseline population.

entry.title: Circular interval-valued regression with application to wind direction: A cylindrical approach

link.title: Circular interval-valued regression with application to wind direction: A cylindrical approach

entry.content: Many real-world datasets are inherently interval-valued, yet standard statistical methods are typically designed for point observations. Furthermore, intervals that are circular in nature may naturally exist. In this paper, we introduce a cylindrical regression framework for interval-valued circular data, addressing the joint challenges of the periodical nature and measurement uncertainty within the observed circular intervals. The proposed model accommodates a circular interval-valued response variable and both circular and linear covariates using a centre-range approach. To estimate the model, a maximum likelihood approach is proposed. The performance of the proposed estimation procedure is demonstrated through a simulation study. Application to two real-world datasets from a wind farm in South Africa and a weather station in Brazil further substantiates the model’s practical value.

entry.title: Locally Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Polynomial Chaos Expansions

link.title: Locally Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Polynomial Chaos Expansions

entry.content: This work develops a locally adaptive jackknife+ conformal prediction framework for polynomial chaos expansions. Therein, the non-conformity scores are normalized with an auxiliary polynomial chaos expansion trained on the log-transformed leave-one-out residuals of the base model. We show that the coverage guarantee of jackknife+ conformal prediction carries over to the adaptive intervals if the leave-one-out auxiliary models are trained on nested leave-one-out residuals. For fixed-basis polynomial chaos expansions fitted by ordinary least squares, all required quantities are derived in closed form and the guarantee-preserving adaptive intervals are obtained from a single model fit, without any model retraining. For sparse polynomial chaos expansions, where multiple model fits are necessary, we propose a heuristic simplification that limits the computational overhead of adaptivity at the cost of the formal coverage guarantee. Numerical experiments on an academic benchmark with known heteroscedastic noise and on an engineering simulation dataset show that the suggested method attains the target coverage while providing intervals that adapt to local prediction uncertainty, therefore being considerably more statistically efficient. These advantages are particularly prominent in high-uncertainty regions of the input space, where the performance of non-adaptive methods degrades substantially.

entry.title: Local Inference for High-dimensional Time Series

link.title: Local Inference for High-dimensional Time Series

entry.content: Local stationarity provides a natural framework for time series whose dependence structure evolves smoothly over time. In high-dimensional settings, however, its classical definition can break down, as approximation errors accumulate across time-varying coefficients. To address this limitation, we introduce $(\epsilon_n,\delta)$-stationarity, a generalization of local stationarity that holds locally in time and allows approximation errors to grow with the dimension, and we combine it with local sparsity, which lets the set of relevant predictors change over time. We show that, for high-dimensional time-varying autoregressions, the rate of stationary approximation is driven by local sparsity, so that local sparsity governs not only estimation but also the stationary approximation itself. We then develop a \textit{local lasso} with time-varying penalties that selects relevant predictors and their periods of activity, and we derive error bounds that depend on the local sparsity, quantify the cost of nonstationarity, and guide penalty and bandwidth selection. For inference, we propose a desparsified local lasso based on local nodewise regressions and establish a linear representation with an explicit smoothing bias. Asymptotic normality then follows under two bandwidth conditions, one for coefficient variation and one for nonstationarity. Simulations and applications to macroeconomic and neuroscience data illustrate the methods.

entry.title: Calibrating demand models versus adjusting OD matrices with traffic counts: a controlled comparison

link.title: Calibrating demand models versus adjusting OD matrices with traffic counts: a controlled comparison

entry.content: Traffic counts are routinely used to calibrate travel demand models, particularly when the origin-destination (OD) matrix is not observed directly. An important modelling decision is whether to adjust individual OD flows or the parameters of the demand model that generates them. The latter approach uses fewer parameters and preserves a relationship between zonal characteristics and demand, but its accuracy depends on the assumed model structure. We compare three established approaches using the same prior information, traffic counts and equilibrium assignment. They estimate five production-gravity coefficients, origin and destination adjustment factors, or individual OD flows. Synthetic experiments on the Eastern Massachusetts and Chicago Sketch networks allow recovery to be assessed against known demand under different forms of model misspecification. Calibrating the five-coefficient model gives better OD recovery and held-out link-flow prediction when demand follows its assumptions or a two-purpose gravity process. Its advantage declines or reverses when destination choice or production relationships vary across zones. Cellwise adjustment achieves the closest fit to calibration counts in 65 of 66 evaluated conditions, yet it recovers OD demand least accurately of the three approaches in 45 of them. These findings show that model parameterisation matters beyond calibration fit. For transport planning, traffic counts should be used alongside independent evidence on trip production and distribution when selecting and validating a demand model.

entry.title: A Generalized Bayesian Approach to Clustering with Dimension Reduction

link.title: A Generalized Bayesian Approach to Clustering with Dimension Reduction

entry.content: Generalized Bayes product partition models provide a probabilistic counterpart to loss-based clustering. They update a prior over partitions through an exponentiated clustering loss rather than a likelihood, so allocation uncertainty can be quantified without a full generative model for the data. However, their performance depends on the space in which the loss is evaluated. For high-dimensional observations, a squared Euclidean loss on the raw features can be dominated by irrelevant coordinates or fail to reflect cluster structure lying near a nonlinear low-dimensional manifold. We propose an extension in which an autoencoder and the partition are learned together, so that the space in which the clustering loss is evaluated is shaped by the clustering itself. Our generalized posterior combines a reconstruction loss, which keeps the low-dimensional representation faithful to the observed data, with a within-cluster sum of squares in the latent representation, which encourages cluster separation. Posterior computation alternates between Gibbs sampling over partitions and gradient-based updates of the autoencoder network, with the learning rate estimated jointly. We illustrate the approach through simulation studies and applications to four benchmark datasets.

entry.content: Vehicle telematics provides detailed observations of driving behaviour that can be useful for automobile insurance risk assessment. Existing approaches often summarize these data through counts of harsh events or individually unusual observations, although driving movements naturally develop over time. Building on a previously proposed hidden Markov model (HMM) framework that identifies pointwise anomalies, we identify short intervals in which a sequence of observations is unusual when considered together. We then examine the original acceleration signals to measure the magnitude and temporal concentration of these episodes and identify recurring patterns of vehicle movement. Temporal concentration describes whether acceleration activity is distributed evenly across an episode or concentrated in relatively few observations. Using a controlled telematics dataset containing normal, aggressive, and drowsy driving by the same drivers, we evaluate the proposed measures through comparisons matched by driver and road type. We find that statistical anomaly measures depend on the driving population used to train the HMM. entry.title: Box-Cox Transformations of Correlation Matrices

link.title: Box-Cox Transformations of Correlation Matrices

entry.content: We consider Box-Cox transformations of correlation matrices, $\Phi_\alpha(C)=\mathrm{vecl}{(C^{\alpha}-I)/\alpha}$, with Jacobian $J_\alpha$. The family nests the raw correlations at $\alpha=1$, the generalised Fisher transformation (GFT), $C\mapsto\mathrm{vecl}(\log C)$, at $\alpha=0$, and the negated off-diagonal concentration coordinates at $\alpha=-1$. The inverse problem is a strictly convex program for every $\alpha$, so every member is injective. The map is onto $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, $d=n(n-1)/2$, if and only if $\alpha\le0$, such that $\alpha=0$ defines the boundary for unrestricted parametrizations. For $\alpha>0$ the image is bounded. The conditioning obeys the bound $\kappa(J_\alpha)\le\kappa(C)^{ 1-\alpha }$, where $\kappa(C)=\lambda_{\max}(C)/\lambda_{\min}(C)$, and on the surjective range the exponent is smallest at $\alpha=0$. Under Gaussian sampling with $n\geq3$, the asymptotic covariance of the transformed sample correlations is the identity at independence for every member, but only $\alpha=0$ retains the identity to first order in the correlations, whereas the leading joint third cumulant at independence vanishes only at $\alpha=1/3$. Finally, applying the transformation to the diagonal rescaling of $C$ that makes the result hollow adds a new family to the existing correlation parametrizations. For every $\alpha$ the rescaling solves a strictly convex problem and the inverse is explicit, and the scaled coordinates are unrestricted exactly when $\alpha=0$, where they recover the known global normal coordinates, centred at independence, for the efficient information metric of the correlations.

entry.title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents

link.title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents

entry.content: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent’s trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent’s current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent’s future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.

entry.title: The Cost of Coverage: Conformalising Native Forecast Uncertainty for GB Wind Power

link.title: The Cost of Coverage: Conformalising Native Forecast Uncertainty for GB Wind Power

entry.content: Uncertainty bands on wind forecasts help inform reserve sizing and commitments, but often fail to deliver their stated coverage. We apply conformal prediction to native bands to see what it adds and what it costs, comparing six forecasters, from ARIMA to a tabular foundation model, at two wind farms in Great Britain (GB) under operational conditions. We show that calibration repairs empirical marginal coverage with little or no Winkler Score penalty, but this apparent success conceals under-coverage in high winds. Calibrating by forecast wind regime turns marginal coverage into regime-level coverage, cutting day-ahead out-of-band volume in high winds by over 40% relative to pooled calibration while narrowing bands overall.

entry.title: Bayesian MI-LASSO for Variable Selection on Multiply-Imputed Data

link.title: Bayesian MI-LASSO for Variable Selection on Multiply-Imputed Data

entry.content: Multiple imputation is widely used for handling missing data in real-world applications. For variable selection on multiply-imputed datasets, however, if selection is performed on each imputed dataset separately, it can result in different sets of selected variables across datasets. MI-LASSO, one of the most commonly used approaches to this problem, regards the same variable across all separate imputed datasets as a group variable and exploits the group LASSO to yield a consistent variable selection across all the multiply-imputed datasets. In this paper, we extend MI-LASSO into the Bayesian framework and propose four Bayesian MI-LASSO models for variable selection on multiply-imputed data, including three shrinkage prior-based and one Spike-and-Slab prior-based methods. To overcome the limitations of traditional, ad hoc threshold-based model selection, we develop a principled four-step projection predictive procedure that provides robust variable selection. This procedure also facilitates approximately calibrated post-selection inference and attains near-nominal coverage under a correct selection model. Simulation studies showed that the Bayesian MI-LASSO outperformed MI-LASSO and other alternative approaches, achieving higher specificity and lower mean squared error across a range of settings. We further demonstrated these methods via a case study using a multiply-imputed dataset from the University of Michigan Dioxin Exposure Study. The R package BMIselect is available on CRAN.

entry.title: Detection of evolutionary shifts in variance under an Ornsten-Uhlenbeck model

link.title: Detection of evolutionary shifts in variance under an Ornsten-Uhlenbeck model

entry.content: Sudden changes in environmental conditions can lead to evolutionary shifts not only in the optimal trait value (theta), but also in the diffusion variance (sigma^2) under the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model. While several methods have been developed to detect shifts in optimal values, few explicitly account for concurrent shifts in both evolutionary variance and diffusion variance. We use a multi-optima and multi-variance OU model to describe trait evolution with shifts in both theta and sigma^2, and analyze how covariance between species is affected when shifts in variance occur along the phylogeny. We propose a new method that simultaneously detects shifts in both variance and optimal values by formulating the problem as a variable selection task using an L1-penalized loss function. Our method is implemented in the R package ShiVa (Detection of evolutionary shifts in variance). Through simulations, we compare ShiVa with existing methods that can automatically detect evolutionary shifts under the OU model (l1ou, PhylogeneticEM, and PCMFit). Our method demonstrates improved predictive ability and significantly reduces false positives in detecting optimal value shifts when variance shifts are present. When only shifts in optimal value occur, our method performs comparably to existing approaches. We apply ShiVa to empirical data on floral diameter in Rafflesiaceae (with Euphorbiaceae outgroups) and buccal morphology in Centrarchidae sunfishes.

entry.title: Causal inference for N-of-1 trials

link.title: Causal inference for N-of-1 trials

entry.content: The aim of personalized medicine is to tailor treatment decisions to individuals’ characteristics. N-of-1 trials are within-person crossover trials that hold the promise of targeting individual-specific effects. While the idea behind N-of-1 trials might seem simple, analyzing and interpreting N-of-1 trials is not straightforward. Here we ground N-of-1 trials in a formal causal inference framework and formalize intuitive claims from the N-of-1 trials literature. We focus on causal inference from a single N-of-1 trial and define a conditional average treatment effect (CATE) that represents a target in this setting, which we call the U-CATE. We discuss assumptions sufficient for identification and estimation of the U-CATE under different causal models where the treatment schedule is assigned at baseline. A simple mean difference is an unbiased, asymptotically normal estimator of the U-CATE in simple settings. We also consider settings where carryover effects, trends over time, time-varying common causes of the outcome, and outcome-outcome effects are present. In these more complex settings, we show that a time-varying g-formula identifies the U-CATE under explicit assumptions. Finally, we analyze data from N-of-1 trials about acne symptoms and show how different assumptions about the data generating process can lead to different analytical strategies.

entry.title: Online conformal inference for multi-step time series forecasting

link.title: Online conformal inference for multi-step time series forecasting

entry.content: We study the construction of distribution-free prediction intervals for multi-step time series forecasting. In this setting, forecast errors at different horizons are serially dependent, and feedback is delayed, since the error of an h-step-ahead forecast becomes available only after h periods. We propose autocorrelated multi-step conformal prediction (AcMCP), an online procedure that accommodates delayed feedback and explicitly incorporates the dependence among multi-step forecast errors into conformal calibration. To characterize this dependence, we derive first-order representations of the optimal forecast errors under a general nonstationary autoregressive data-generating process, with explicit bounds on remainder terms. AcMCP guarantees long-run coverage of at least the nominal level at every horizon, without requiring exchangeability or any assumption on how the data distribution evolves over time. We also establish a finite-sample bound on the empirical coverage shortfall, which depends on the forecast horizon and the evaluation sample size. Notably, these guarantees do not rely on the accuracy of the linear approximations. Simulations and real-data applications show that AcMCP adapts to time-varying dynamics and maintains rolling coverage close to the nominal level. By exploiting the dependence among multi-step errors, it often yields narrower intervals than its counterpart without this dependence, with similar coverage, particularly at longer horizons.

entry.title: Likelihood-free Posterior Density Learning for Uncertainty Quantification in Inference Problems

link.title: Likelihood-free Posterior Density Learning for Uncertainty Quantification in Inference Problems

entry.content: Generative models and those with computationally intractable likelihoods are widely used to describe complex systems in the natural sciences, social sciences, and engineering. Fitting these models to data requires likelihood-free inference methods that explore the parameter space without explicit likelihood evaluations, relying instead on sequential simulation, which comes at the cost of computational efficiency and extensive tuning. We develop an alternative framework called kernel-adaptive synthetic posterior estimation (KASPE) that uses deep learning to directly reconstruct the mapping between the observed data and a finite-dimensional parametric representation of the posterior distribution, trained on a large number of simulated datasets. We provide theoretical justification for KASPE and a formal connection to the likelihood-based approach of expectation propagation. Simulation experiments demonstrate KASPE’s flexibility and performance relative to existing likelihood-free methods including approximate Bayesian computation in challenging inferential settings involving posteriors with heavy tails, multiple local modes, and over the parameters of a nonlinear dynamical system.

entry.title: Stochastic Derivative Estimation for Discontinuous Sample Performances: A Leibniz Integration Perspective

link.title: Stochastic Derivative Estimation for Discontinuous Sample Performances: A Leibniz Integration Perspective

entry.content: Based on the multidimensional Leibniz integral rule, we propose a novel unbiased stochastic derivative estimation framework for sample performance functions that are discontinuous in the parameter of interest. In this framework, for general discontinuities, a change of variables followed by the Leibniz integral rule generally yields a multi-run estimator, whereas for indicator-type discontinuities, a suitable transformation of the sample performance leads directly to a single-run estimator. The new framework includes existing likelihood ratio (LR)-based approaches as special cases and applies more broadly. In particular, it encompasses generalized LR (GLR) methods and the new formulation permits us to obtain much milder and simpler sufficient regularity conditions for these estimators to be unbiased, compared with the conditions given in previous papers. We also provide guidance on how to construct efficient single-run estimators in settings where existing methods may require the simulation of multiple sample paths or may be inapplicable. We validate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework through an inventory-price control problem.

entry.title: Beyond Maximum Likelihood: Variational Inequality Estimation for Generalized Linear Models

link.title: Beyond Maximum Likelihood: Variational Inequality Estimation for Generalized Linear Models

entry.content: Generalized linear models (GLMs) are fundamental tools for statistical modeling, with maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) serving as the classical approach for parameter inference. While MLE performs well for canonical GLMs, it can become computationally challenging in more general settings with non-canonical, non-smooth, or saturating link functions, where the resulting optimization landscape may be ill-conditioned, non-convex, or non-differentiable. In this paper, we study an alternative estimation framework based on variational inequalities (VIs), which formulates GLM estimation through an operator-based equilibrium condition rather than likelihood minimization. We analyze the VI estimator from a statistical perspective and establish finite-sample error bounds and asymptotic normality, together with convergence guarantees for fixed-point and stochastic approximation algorithms. The framework accommodates a broad class of link functions, including non-canonical, non-smooth, and non-monotone cases satisfying a strong Minty-type condition, and extends naturally to generalized additive models (GAMs) via basis expansion. Numerical experiments demonstrate that under a fixed iteration budget, the VI approach achieves competitive estimation accuracy and faster, more stable convergence than MLE, particularly in GLMs and GAMs with non-canonical or non-smooth link functions.

entry.title: A Poisson Factor Mixture Model for the Analysis of Linguistic Competence

link.title: A Poisson Factor Mixture Model for the Analysis of Linguistic Competence

entry.content: Dependence among variables and unobserved heterogeneity are common features of multivariate count data. We propose a model-based clustering approach for this setting based on a Poisson factor mixture model, which combines a low-dimensional latent structure with a finite mixture specification. This enables simultaneous dimension reduction and clustering while providing interpretable latent representations of count profiles. The proposal originates from the UniversITA project, which collected formal written texts from a representative sample of Italian university students. Since university students play a central role in the process of linguistic change, as they are the most educated segment of the youth population, understanding variation in their writing is substantively important for both language research and higher education policy. Texts were annotated for various linguistic features, producing multivariate count data. The fitted model identifies two correlated latent dimensions of writing competence, interpretable as communicative effectiveness and grammatical-linguistic control. Incorporating educational and sociodemographic covariates further reveals distinct student profiles associated with field of study and prior educational background. Beyond this application, the proposed framework can be employed for the analysis of heterogeneous multivariate count data with complex dependence patterns, such as those arising in educational assessments, psychological and behavioral studies, and text analysis.

entry.title: Proxy-Reliance Control in Conformal Recalibration of One-Sided Value-at-Risk

link.title: Proxy-Reliance Control in Conformal Recalibration of One-Sided Value-at-Risk

entry.content: We introduce a proxy-reliance-controlled conformal recalibration framework for one-sided Value-at-Risk (VaR), and study a question that existing state-aware methods do not usually isolate: how strongly should the recalibration adjustment depend on an imperfect volatility proxy? We formalize this through a proxy-reliance parameter that continuously interpolates between an approximately constant-shift correction and a fully proxy-scaled correction. This makes proxy reliance a distinct and practically interpretable design choice in one-sided VaR recalibration. We show theoretically that larger proxy reliance increases the responsiveness of the tail adjustment to proxy scale, but also increases stressed-state fragility when the proxy underreacts. Empirically, in rolling out-of-sample tests on a six-ETF panel with VIX-linked state variables, and with supporting evidence from SPY, we find that the empirical value of proxy-reliance control lies in improved stressed-state robustness rather than uniform overall dominance. In particular, when the baseline forecast remains exposed to proxy imperfection in stressed states, lower or intermediate proxy reliance can outperform fully proxy-scaled recalibration in stressed left-tail VaR control.

entry.title: From multilayer networks to covariates: Layer-specific community detection

link.title: From multilayer networks to covariates: Layer-specific community detection

entry.content: We study layer-specific community detection in multilayer networks with heterogeneous community memberships and degree distributions. Membership mismatch complicates cross-layer information pooling, whereas sparsity heterogeneity can provide complementary signals for poorly connected communities. We recast the problem as network-with-covariates clustering: the target layer is retained as the primary network, while the remaining layers are converted into nodal covariates through our regularized spectral construction approach. We then perform community detection using a node-adaptive balancing scheme that relies more on the target network for high-degree nodes and more on the constructed covariates for low-degree nodes. Under a multilayer degree-corrected stochastic blockmodel, we establish guarantees for the constructed covariates and weak consistency when the average membership mismatch vanishes. Under additional degree structure and node-specific mismatch conditions, we establish strong consistency while allowing the average membership mismatch to remain nonvanishing. entry.content: Randomized experiments have long been the gold standard for scientists seeking to learn about cause and effect. entry.title: Improving Minority Population Sampling with BISG Probabilities: Evidence from a Survey of Jewish Americans

link.title: Improving Minority Population Sampling with BISG Probabilities: Evidence from a Survey of Jewish Americans

entry.content: Sampling geographically dispersed minority populations poses substantial challenges when individual group membership cannot be directly observed. Although stratified sampling can offer efficiency gains, these gains are typically modest unless the minority population is highly concentrated within a small number of strata. In this paper, we propose using Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG) to enhance the efficiency of minority population sampling. BISG generates individual-level probabilities of minority group membership based on names and residential addresses. We incorporate these probabilities into a stratified Poisson probability sampling design. Applying the proposed approach to a national survey of Jewish Americans, we find that our estimates closely align with those from a large-scale Pew Research Center survey of the same population, which relied on a substantially more expensive sampling strategy involving geographic stratification and screening. At a fraction of the cost, our survey reproduces nearly identical patterns observed by Pew, including estimates of religious denomination prevalence and participation in specific religious activities.

entry.title: Empirical Bayes Rebiasing

link.title: Empirical Bayes Rebiasing

entry.content: We study methods for simultaneous analysis of many noisy and biased estimates, each paired with an even noisier estimate of its own bias. The analyst’s goal is to construct short calibrated intervals for each parameter. The standard debiasing approach, which subtracts the bias estimate from each biased estimate, inflates variance and yields long intervals. We provide convergence rates for the coverage of our intervals when the bias distribution is estimated using nonparametric maximum likelihood. Furthermore, we demonstrate substantial precision gains in prediction-powered inference, including pairwise LLM win-rate evaluations, as well as for inference of direct genetic effects in family-based GWAS.

entry.title: An Energy-Driven Framework for Privacy-Aware Synthetic Data Generation

link.title: An Energy-Driven Framework for Privacy-Aware Synthetic Data Generation

entry.content: Access to microdata in official statistics requires balancing disclosure risk and statistical utility. This paper proposes an interpretable, open-box energy-driven framework for privacy-aware synthesis of mixed-type tabular data, combining discriminative modelling, Bayesian-network proposals, Metropolis–Hastings sampling and post-generation optimization. Explicit energy components govern record-level plausibility, proximity to training records and diversity, while target selection balances fidelity and classification utility, making these trade-offs directly inspectable. Evaluation uses an artificially constructed individual-level dataset with demographic, behavioural and health-related variables. Validation combines marginal, bivariate and conditional fidelity diagnostics, diversity measures, nearest-neighbour analyses and membership inference attacks. An arrangement of classifiers trained on reference and synthetic data is evaluated on a common reference holdout. Repeated target selection assesses stability within a fixed candidate pool. Results show a convincing trade-off between fidelity and utility of the synthetic data generated by means of the proposed framework. Membership attacks perform close to chance across repeated splits, indicating limited training-membership discrimination under the evaluated protocol. The findings support the feasibility of balancing fidelity, utility and privacy-aware objectives through explicit generation and selection criteria, without implying formal privacy guarantees.

entry.title: U-centering as subset ANOVA: edge regression and higher-order theory

link.title: U-centering as subset ANOVA: edge regression and higher-order theory

entry.content: Unbiased squared distance covariance and the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (HSIC) are fourth-order U-statistics, yet U-centering evaluates them from pairwise arrays in $O(n^2)$ operations. We show that U-centering is exactly least-squares residualization after fitting additive endpoint effects. This analysis of variance (ANOVA) interpretation explains the zero row sums and the normalization through residual degrees of freedom. The same geometry gives regression representations of dependence and two-sample statistics, exact permutation variances, and relations among pooled and regression mean squares. For arrays indexed by $r$-element subsets and $n\ge2r$, higher-order U-centering removes all lower-order subset effects and projects onto a space of dimension $\binom{n}{r}-\binom{n}{r-1}$. For fixed symmetric square-integrable kernels evaluated on independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) paired observations, we derive the residual covariance matrix, exact mean-squared errors for estimating the highest-order Hoeffding components, unbiased positive semidefinite (PSD) covariance estimates, and moment formulas under independence and permutation. The normalized residual inner product equals a direct unbiased estimator involving up to $2r$ observations, but can be evaluated in $O(n^r)$ operations for fixed $r$. For four-argument matching kernels, three matrix products yield exactly unbiased estimators of a fourth spectral moment of kernel cross-covariance in $O(n^3)$ arithmetic and $O(n^2)$ storage. A numerical illustration distinguishes dependence structures with equal HSIC and different spectral concentration.

entry.title: The Earth Moves, But So Does the Bias: Systematic Upward Bias of the Wasserstein (Earth Mover’s) Distance and Permutation-Based Null Calibration

link.title: The Earth Moves, But So Does the Bias: Systematic Upward Bias of the Wasserstein (Earth Mover’s) Distance and Permutation-Based Null Calibration

entry.content: The Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) is gaining increasing interest among political scientists for assessing similarity in preference distributions. Existing applications predominantly involve relatively large samples and low-dimensional response spaces, which can mitigate finite-sample distortions. However, empirical EMD remains biased upward due to sampling variation in empirical probability measures. This problem is often overlooked and becomes especially severe in high-dimensional or sparse settings, including conjoint distributions that serve as an illustrative example in this paper. As political scientists are broadening their use cases of EMD, this paper cautions against interpreting standard bootstrap uncertainty bounds as a correction for the upward bias of empirical EMD. It proposes a permutation-based null calibration framework for more robust hypothesis testing. As a non-parametric approach, it frees researchers from making directional or distributional shape assumptions. While alternative estimators require these rigid assumptions to correct for upward bias, political science data often fail to meet them in practice. Through four sets of Monte Carlo simulations, this paper demonstrates the utility of this framework. The proposed approach also applies more generally to empirical comparisons of two probability distributions defined on a common metric space, provided that the ground distance between support points is substantively meaningful.

entry.title: Estimating Treatment Effects Through Intermediate-Event Pathways with Multi-State Data

link.title: Estimating Treatment Effects Through Intermediate-Event Pathways with Multi-State Data

entry.content: During clinical trials evaluating a drug’s effect on a survival endpoint, intermediate events often occur before the primary event. The treatment can affect the primary event through multiple pathways via intermediate events. With multiple intermediate events, each is a treatment-induced confounder of transitions out of the others, so we cannot identify natural or separable effects. We instead consider stochastic interventions that assign each transition the identifiable observed-history hazard of either arm. Contrasts between the resulting counterfactual cumulative incidences define transition-, event-, and path-targeted effects, identifiable without cross-world or isolation assumptions. Based on the efficient influence functions for the counterfactual cumulative incidences under hypothetical interventions, we construct multiply robust and semiparametrically efficient estimators for these targeted treatment effects. Our proposed framework quantifies treatment effects through each transition, on each event, and along each path. By analyzing data from the LEADER trial, we find that liraglutide significantly reduces the risk of cardiovascular and microvascular events. The reduction in all-cause mortality is primarily mediated by its effects on expanded major adverse cardiovascular events.

entry.title: A Latent-Space Statistical Learning Framework for Semicontinuous Outcomes: Regularized Deviance and Boundary-Stabilized Optimization

link.title: A Latent-Space Statistical Learning Framework for Semicontinuous Outcomes: Regularized Deviance and Boundary-Stabilized Optimization

entry.content: Semicontinuous outcomes characterized by an exact zero mass and heavy-tailed continuous distributions challenge empirical risk modeling and machine learning. Compound Poisson-Gamma Tweedie processes impose a rigid mean-variance coupling that distorts zero-mass probabilities under extreme tail dispersion, flattening continuous density and reducing extreme-risk discrimination. Furthermore, heuristic post-hoc target capping introduces systematic bias while leaving loss gradients vulnerable to tail leverage. We present a unified, statistically coherent likelihood framework for semicontinuous modeling under arbitrary zero-inflation and explicit upper boundary constraints. Optimization and likelihood evaluations operate strictly in a latent space defined by the power-scaling mapping $y_i^* = \min{(y_i/s)^\lambda, U^*}$, where $s \in (0, U)$ anchors scale and $\lambda \in (0,1)$ regularizes tail curvature. The architecture partitions the response into three regimes: an unconstrained Bernoulli hurdle, an analytical continuous Gamma body, and an upper boundary point mass governed by incomplete Gamma survival ratios. Rather than an arbitrary truncation, the boundary functions as an intrinsic tail accumulator bounding score and Hessian dynamics. We derive the closed-form deviance objective, score vectors, and block-diagonal Hessian matrix, proving that parameter spaces are information-orthogonal to enable concurrent classification and regression updates. Asymptotic boundary analysis demonstrates that score and curvature scale linearly in the deep tail, establishing a quadratic restoring force that prevents gradient collapse. The framework breaks the Tweedie parameter rigidity paradox while maintaining structural fidelity across both zero occurrence and extreme severity differentiation.

link.title: Counterexamples and Sufficient Conditions: Comments on “Optimally-Transported Generalized Method of Moments”

entry.content: We comment on the optimally-transported generalized method of moments (OTGMM) of Schennach and Starck (2026) and give counterexamples to Theorems 2-6. In the small-error analysis, the assumptions do not ensure consistency or asymptotic normality (Theorems 2-3). In the large-error analysis, Theorem 4 states the equivalence between the OTGMM estimator and the GMM estimator with modified moments, and Theorems 5-6 assert consistency and asymptotic normality. Through counterexamples, we show that the equivalence in Theorem 4 fails and a component of the Lagrange multiplier has different limits under the two estimators (Theorems 5-6). We also point out that, under misspecification, the population value selected by OTGMM depends on the metric. We give sufficient conditions and establish results following the original motivation for OTGMM. Our corrections to Theorems 4-6 change their assumptions or interpretation more substantially than those to Theorems 2 and 3. Furthermore, we correct Assumption 16 and the test’s null distribution.

entry.content: Many real-world high-dimensional time series exhibit long-memory, but Gaussian graphical model testing in this regime remains understudied. We develop a direct, data-adaptive test statistic for assessing conditional independence in the graph structure of stationary Gaussian time series. We establish a finite-sample, Berry–Esseen type Gaussian approximation bound for the statistic, which applies to both short-memory and long-memory time series. The testing procedure uses a block bootstrap method, on which we provide a finite-sample validity result including in the ultra-high-dimensional scenario, and can be extended to comparing graphical structures in two-sample tests. We also develop a consistency-empowered correction to the statistic and show that such tests attain asymptotic consistency in both size and power. Our proposed method is applied to real-world fMRI data to understand functional connectivities within brain in different periods.

entry.title: Quantifying Inconsistent Mediation: The Mediated Magnitude Share and the Degree of Suppression

link.title: Quantifying Inconsistent Mediation: The Mediated Magnitude Share and the Degree of Suppression

entry.content: The proportion mediated (PM), the indirect effect divided by the total effect, is intuitive when direct and indirect effects act in the same direction. Under inconsistent mediation, however, opposing pathways partially cancel, so PM can fall outside the unit interval and becomes unstable as the total effect approaches zero. We propose two complementary effect-scale measures: the mediated magnitude share (MMS), which quantifies the absolute magnitude of an indirect pathway relative to the combined absolute magnitudes of the direct and indirect pathways, and the degree of suppression, which quantifies the fraction of this combined magnitude cancelled by opposing pathways. Both measures are bounded between 0 and 1, and MMS reduces to PM under consistent mediation. We extend both measures to multiple indirect pathways and, through a logarithmic transformation, to binary outcomes on ratio scales. In simulations with continuous and binary outcomes, PM estimates were highly dispersed when the total effect was small relative to the pathway magnitudes, whereas estimates of MMS and the degree of suppression remained bounded. We illustrate the measures using previously published estimates from the Adolescents Training and Learning to Avoid Steroids (ATLAS) program, where PM was $-0.30$, MMS was $0.19$, and the degree of suppression was $0.38$, showing how the two measures describe the relative pathway magnitudes and their cancellation under inconsistent mediation.

entry.title: GPU-accelerated Regularized Vector Multiplicative Error Models for Positive-valued Financial Time Series

link.title: GPU-accelerated Regularized Vector Multiplicative Error Models for Positive-valued Financial Time Series

entry.content: The logarithmic vector multiplicative error model (log-vMEM) provides a methodology for modeling and forecasting multivariate positive-valued time series. However, the number of autoregressive parameters increases rapidly with the system dimension and lag order, posing challenges for estimation and model selection. This paper develops a regularized estimation framework for the log-vMEM with multivariate Gamma errors by incorporating hierarchical lag structures to induce sparsity and accommodate heterogeneous lag dynamics. We consider three hierarchical lag structures: componentwise, own-other, and elementwise, in combination with group lasso, group MCP, and group SCAD, adaptive group lasso penalties. Parameter estimation is carried out through an alternating block-coordinate optimization algorithm with sequential Gauss-Seidel updates, while GPU-accelerated numerical quadrature is employed to address the computational burden of evaluating the multivariate Gamma likelihood. Simulation experiments investigate parameter recovery and lag selection under different sparsity structures. The real data analysis is carried out on the realized volatility measures for Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) which allows a comparison of the competing regularization approaches in an empirical financial setting. Together, these developments provide a computational framework for sparse multivariate volatility modeling with flexible lag structures and dependent Gamma errors.

entry.title: When Statisticians Can Also Be AI Engineers, What Could We Build?

link.title: When Statisticians Can Also Be AI Engineers, What Could We Build?

entry.content: Statistical software makes methods widely available. Good statistical work, however, requires understanding the question, how the data were collected, and what conclusions the evidence can support. As AI agents make data analysis accessible to people without statistical training, this reasoning should be built into the systems themselves. Our review of selected AI agents for data analysis and study design points to a gap in documented support for scientific inquiry with users at runtime. In this paper, we advocate designing domain-specific interactive harnesses in which statistical principles guide proactive inquiry: agents recognize missing information that could change an analysis, ask questions users may not know to raise, and use the answers to guide or revise analytical decisions. entry.title: A Hybrid Framework for Explainable Aviation Risk: Causal Chain Extraction from Safety Reports with Physics-Based Failure Quantification and Interventional Analysis

link.title: A Hybrid Framework for Explainable Aviation Risk: Causal Chain Extraction from Safety Reports with Physics-Based Failure Quantification and Interventional Analysis

entry.content: Aviation authorities hold decades of accident reports whose narratives record how investigators reconstructed each accident. Computational work on these archives has mostly sorted reports into fixed taxonomies. In this work, we propose a hybrid framework in which a text-based corpus identifies the leading factors of a failure mode. Physics-based models then quantify how likely that failure is at a stated operating point. Ordered causal chains extracted from 56{,}202 American accident reports with a local large language model aggregate into a causation knowledge graph. On an evaluation sample of 2{,}000 reports, the chains recover 90.8\% of investigator-flagged causes. Each physical factor whose drivers the record carries receives an occurrence model calibrated to the accident population. A leaky noisy-OR fitted to the corpus combines the factors into a failure mode probability that supports intervention. For engine power loss, the carburetor icing model separates 1{,}205 icing accidents from other accidents using temperature and dewpoint alone, reaching 0.61 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve against a density ratio ceiling of 0.64. Routine weather hours give no valid control, because flying concentrates in fair weather. On later years the physics adds 0.03 to that area for occurrence and nothing for severity, so its value lies in interpretability. On four named accidents, abduction gives a probability of necessity of 0.29 to 0.50 for the heat omission, under monotonicity. The Fast Causal Inference algorithm does not license the largest backdoor adjustment on the learned networks.

entry.title: dsp: An R Package for Bayesian Time Series Modeling with the Dynamic Shrinkage Process

link.title: dsp: An R Package for Bayesian Time Series Modeling with the Dynamic Shrinkage Process

entry.content: dsp provides a unified state-space framework for modeling nonstationary time series using the Dynamic Shrinkage Process (DSP), a class of global-local shrinkage priors. DSP adaptively regularizes time-varying parameters to shrink noise while preserving abrupt changes and other local structure. The package supports Gaussian and count-data smoothing, changepoint detection, time-varying parameter regression, and volatility estimation, with posterior predictive draws available for missing-value imputation and forecasting. Nonstationary time series often contain periods of relative stability punctuated by abrupt changes in mean or variance. dsp offers a common interface for model specification, posterior computation, summarization, and visualization across models that were previously developed separately in the literature. Core functionality is implemented in C++ via Rcpp for computational efficiency. We describe the underlying models, package design, and the main functions for fitting, summarizing, and plotting posterior results.

entry.title: Sample size calculation comparing two survival curves in the presence of nonproportional hazards utilizing the concept of Weighted Relative Time using two different Weibull distributions

link.title: Sample size calculation comparing two survival curves in the presence of nonproportional hazards utilizing the concept of Weighted Relative Time using two different Weibull distributions

entry.content: Sample size calculations in two-arm clinical trials with survival endpoint often utilize the proportional hazards (PH) assumption. In case of nonproportional hazards (NPH), much research is ongoing with some newer methods developed that work well in specific scenarios. Recent developments have considered the nonparametric Max-Combo logrank test for both design and analysis of survival data with NPH. Although many approaches have been proposed for analyzing time-to-event data with NPH such as Restricted Mean Survival Time, Average Hazard Ratios, and piecewise exponential model with hazard ratios changing over time, translation into sample size calculation is not obvious and relies on simulations for very specific scenarios of NPH. In the parametric setting, accelerated failure time models that allow NPH but require a constant time ratio assumption (PT assumption) have been proposed. Recently, a parametric approach that simultaneously allows both nonproportional hazards (NPH) and nonproportional time (NPT) has been proposed. It utilizes the concept of Relative Time (RT) with two different Weibull distributions for the two trial arms in the case of monotonically increasing/decreasing time ratios. A key limitation is that the hypotheses leading to the sample size calculation rely on a single effect size defined at a specific survival percentile. In our current work, we extend the parent RT method by utilizing the concept of Weighted Relative Time (WRT) that allows us comparison of the full survival curves. Performance of the proposed method is compared to the Max-Combo method under different weighting schemes, and its operation characteristics are studied via simulations.

entry.title: Neyman Orthogonalized Specification Tests for Conditional Tail Index Models

link.title: Neyman Orthogonalized Specification Tests for Conditional Tail Index Models

entry.content: We develop specification tests for parametric conditional tail index models of heavy-tailed distributions. The tests are based on a projected empirical process that removes the first-order effect of estimating the null parameter. Within the conditional Hall class, we identify conditions under which projection also eliminates the leading Pareto approximation bias in the test process, permitting lower thresholds while preserving asymptotically correct size. We establish the validity of the tests via multiplier bootstrap. For log-linear models, bootstrap validity extends to settings in which covariates among observations above a common threshold concentrate and the smallest eigenvalue of the information matrix tends to zero. We further propose a data-driven threshold selection rule based on an estimate of the Pareto approximation bias after projection. The rule allows lower thresholds to retain more observations for testing while limiting size distortions, with potential gains in power. The finite sample performance of the tests is examined through simulations and a real data application.

entry.title: Clouded Representatives and Score Matching for Distributed Quantile Regression

link.title: Clouded Representatives and Score Matching for Distributed Quantile Regression

entry.content: Quantile regression is widely used in high-stakes applications where the data are distributed across many sites and the individual records cannot be shared. The existing distributed methods for quantile regression typically require homogeneous sites, large sites, or synchronous communication, which are rarely all satisfied in practice. In this paper, we propose a new method named cloudqr. Each site summarizes its observations by a few Gaussian clouds, each given by the size, center, and covariance of a group of observations, such that the clouds match the score of the raw data exactly. A central server then fits the quantile regression on the clouds from all sites. We establish the convergence of cloudqr under mild conditions. With simulation studies and two real-world applications, we demonstrate the superior performance of cloudqr over the existing distributed methods.

entry.title: When Do Sports Leagues Stop Being Competitive? Bayesian Detection of Competitive-Balance Eras from Match-Level Data

link.title: When Do Sports Leagues Stop Being Competitive? Bayesian Detection of Competitive-Balance Eras from Match-Level Data

entry.content: Competitive balance shapes outcome uncertainty, fan interest, and league regulation, yet standard measures summarize realized standings and cannot separate structural ability differences from match-level randomness. We develop a Bayesian framework that infers structural competitive balance from longitudinal match outcomes. Team abilities are obtained by projecting Gaussian auxiliary variables onto a graph-fused l1 polytope whose radius measures total pairwise ability variation. The projection places positive probability on exact ties, so statistically indistinguishable teams form explicit rank tiers. The radius equals realized ability variation whenever the constraint binds, linking it to parity, detectability, and structural inequality. An adaptive finite-regime model lets competitive eras recur, emerge, and disappear while team hierarchies remain season specific. Simulations show accurate recovery of regimes, radii, abilities, and tiers. Applied to 25 English Premier League seasons, the model identifies a persistent shift to a more stratified league beginning in 2005/06, with 2010/11 the only later return to the compressed regime. It also shows that a close title race can coexist with wide league-wide separation and that head-to-head results can separate clubs level on points. The framework gives leagues a model-based measure of balance to inform debates on revenue sharing and financial regulation.
